content.text: This section sets high standards for teaching practice, in line with the Eduversal Teacher Appraisal System. It promotes reflective, evidence-based teaching through Professional Learning Communities. It supports continuous professional growth through structured induction and mentoring. It brings STEAM education and 21st-century teaching methods into the whole curriculum. It makes sure all students receive high-quality, culturally responsive teaching that maximizes their learning and wellbeing.

steps: All Students Can Learn We hold high expectations for every student, whatever their background, prior achievement, or learning differences. Growth mindset principles guide our approach. We recognize that intelligence and abilities develop through effort, strategy, and support. The teacher's role is to remove barriers, provide scaffolding, and celebrate progress.

Teaching is Both Art and Science Science gives us evidence-based strategies. These come from research on how students learn and on effective teaching methods. Art brings responsiveness to context, relationships, creativity, and cultural awareness. Effective teaching balances structure with flexibility. It adapts proven strategies to meet the unique needs of each classroom.

Learning is Active and Constructive Students learn by doing, thinking, discussing, and creating, not just listening. Teachers guide learning instead of simply passing on information. We emphasize inquiry, problem-solving, collaboration, and STEAM approaches to develop critical thinking and innovation.

Relationships Matter Positive teacher-student relationships are the foundation for learning. Students take risks, keep trying, and take part when they feel safe, valued, and connected. Culturally responsive teaching respects students' identities and experiences, and the diverse Indonesian context of our schools.

Assessment Informs Instruction Teaching and assessment work together; they are not separate processes. Formative assessment tells teachers how to adjust their teaching as the lesson happens. The feedback loop of Teach → Assess → Reflect → Adjust → Re-teach keeps student learning outcomes improving.

Continuous Improvement Through Collaboration Teaching is a profession that needs lifelong learning. Reflective practice means analyzing what works, why, and for whom. Professional growth comes from working with colleagues through PLCs (Professional Learning Communities) and from seeking feedback. It also comes from taking part in the Development of Teaching Proficiency (DTP) program and trying new approaches.

content.text: The Eduversal Teacher Appraisal System is a full, evidence-based framework. It aims to raise teaching quality, support professional development, and improve student learning outcomes across all Eduversal Partner Schools. The system promotes transparency, accountability, and continuous improvement. It also recognizes and rewards effective teaching.
content.title: Purpose

content.text: The annual appraisal cycle has five key phases: Phase 1: Orientation (Beginning of Academic Year) The Eduversal Appraisal Team runs socialization programs. These programs are for school management board members and teachers. They introduce the appraisal timeline, rubrics, and expectations. Each school makes sure all teachers receive an orientation to the system. Teachers also get ongoing support to understand how the rubric is applied. Phase 2: Data Collection Throughout the Year Schools collect evidence continuously through:
content.title: 7.3.1 Appraisal Cycle and Timeline

items: Administrative document reviews
Informal walkthrough observations by school leadership
Evidence from checks of the teacher's work (professional responsibilities)
Student satisfaction surveys (end of each semester)

content.text: Phase 3: Appraisal Visit (scheduled in the academic calendar; both on-site visits fall in Semester 1) The Eduversal Appraisal Team visits each partner school. The team calibrates and validates the school's own appraisal evidence (visit observations are formative-only — see Domain 2 below):

items: Frequency: two Eduversal Appraisal Team visits per year, both in Semester 1. They are the Teaching Quality Visit (Phase 1, August–September) and the Validation Visit (Phase 3, October–November) of the School Appraisal cycle.
Duration: 2 days per school
Activities: Subject appraisals, walkthrough observations, document reviews, post-observation conferences

Cadence and ownership: Eduversal visit observations are formative only (Glow/Grow/Go feedback to the teacher). The school's own appraisers observe each teacher at least 3 times per semester. These appraisers are the Subject Leader/HoD, the Principal, or the Academic/Cambridge Coordinator. Only these school observations feed the F2 (Classroom Observation) score (see Domain 2 below).
Teacher Feedback Sessions: about 30 minutes per observed teacher (same day or following day)
School Management Meeting: 60-90 minutes to review findings across all domains
Oral Exit Report: Presented on the last day of the visit

Written Report: There is no separate written report for each visit. Visit notes go into the school’s Evidence Guide workbook. The cycle’s one written report is the Annual School Quality Report. It is issued within three weeks of the Phase 3 Validation Visit.

content.text: Phase 5: Follow-Through and Professional Growth Planning

items: Final scores and predicates published in EduNav
Individual professional development recommendations
School-wide action planning for areas of growth
Integration with DTP (Development of Teaching Proficiency) program for targeted support

content.text: Scoring Method: School administrators score Domain 3. They base the score on all the evidence gathered throughout the year, not on the appraisal visit observation.

items: Frequency: End of each semester

Confidentiality: Responses are anonymous to encourage honest feedback
Clarity of instruction and explanations

content.text: Each indicator in every domain is rated on a four-level performance rubric:

content.title: Four-Level Performance Rubric
rows: Consistently shows the indicator at the highest level; innovates and shares with colleagues; exceptional student learning outcomes
Regularly demonstrates indicator; minor areas for refinement; strong student learning
Inconsistently demonstrates indicator; gaps in practice; acceptable but uneven student learning
Does not meet expectations; requires intervention
Rarely or never demonstrates indicator; significant gaps; student learning compromised

content.text: Note: Teachers should show Proficient (Level 3) performance on all indicators. This is the baseline expectation for effective teaching. For detailed rubrics with specific indicators for each sub-domain, see Appendix 7-A: Teacher Appraisal Rubrics (Detailed Indicators).

Rating Calculation: Each indicator observed is rated 1-4 based on the rubric.

Domain scores are calculated as follows: Final Score Calculation:

Primary and Secondary: Final Score = (Domain 1 Score × 0.20) + (Domain 2 Score × 0.50) + (Domain 3 Score × 0.20) + (Domain 4 Score × 0.10).

Early Years: Final Score = (Domain 1 Score × 0.20) + (Domain 2 Score × 0.60) + (Domain 3 Score × 0.20). Domain 4 is not administered at Early Years.

Domain scores are the average of all indicators in that domain, on a scale of 1-4. They are then converted to a 0-100 scale for final scoring.

Predicate Assignment: Target Standard: All teachers should achieve at least Predicate B (Good) to show effective teaching in line with Eduversal standards.

Publication of Results:

content.title: Final Score, Predicate and Performance Level

items: Final scores and predicates are calculated from the school's own year-round appraisal records in EduNav. They are published within 2 weeks of the cycle closing. The Eduversal visit contributes calibration and validation, never individual scores.
Individual teacher reports are open to the teacher, mentor, and school leadership

content.text:
Purpose: Build a shared understanding of the lesson context, objectives, and expected student responses before the formal observation.

Participants: Teacher and appraiser (HoD / Subject Leader, Academic or Cambridge Coordinator, or Principal — the school's own appraisers). An Eduversal Specialist may also observe, but only formatively.

Timing: 1-2 days before the scheduled observation (15-20 minutes)

Discussion Topics:
content.title: 7.4.1 Pre-Observation Conference

items: Lesson objectives and alignment to curriculum standards (Cambridge and/or Indonesian CP)
Student context: Where students are in the unit, prior learning, any particular challenges or needs
Instructional strategies planned and rationale
Expected student responses and how the teacher will deal with misconceptions
Assessment methods to be used during lesson
Differentiation strategies for diverse learners (EAL, SEN, advanced)
Teacher's focus area for feedback (e.g., "I want specific feedback on my questioning techniques to promote higher-order thinking")
Lesson plan
Unit overview (optional)
Student work samples or assessment data (optional, to provide context)
Ask questions to understand the teacher's planning and decisions
Discuss observation focus agreed with teacher
Explain observation process and rubric
Set a supportive, collaborative tone (appraisal is there to help you improve, not to catch you out)
The observer arrives quietly and sits in a place that does not draw attention
Minimal disruption to lesson flow
Observer may have printed observation form or digital device for notes
Evidence Collection: Observer takes detailed, objective notes on what teacher and students are doing and saying
Focus Areas: Planning & Organization, Classroom Management, Instructional Process, Assessment (Domain 2 sub-domains)
Rubric Use: The observer refers to the rubric indicators while observing and notes examples of each performance level

Student Interaction (Optional): The observer may ask students what they are learning, look at student work, or ask the teacher short questions to clarify. This is always done respectfully and with as little disruption as possible.
Look for evidence, not judgment: "Teacher used think-pair-share to engage all students" (evidence) vs. "Teacher is good at engagement" (judgment)
Notice patterns: One event does not define a teacher's performance. Look for practices you see again and again
Consider context: EAL (English as an Additional Language) learners, class size, time of day and the resources available
Interrupt the lesson to correct the teacher or to redirect students
Have long conversations while the teacher is teaching
Judge the lesson by personal preferences instead of the rubric criteria
Make quick judgments without enough evidence

content.text:
Purpose: Give good, evidence-based feedback that guides the teacher's professional growth over time.

Timing: The same day or the next day (about 30 minutes). The meeting follows the Glow / Grow / Go protocol.

Structure:

1. Teacher Reflection (5-10 minutes) The teacher shares a self-assessment first:
content.title: 7.4.3 Post-Observation Conference

items: What went well in the lesson?
What would you change if you taught this lesson again?
How did students respond? Did they meet the objectives?
Any surprises or challenges?

content.text:
Rationale: When the teacher reflects first, the teacher takes ownership of their professional growth. It also helps the observer understand the teacher's point of view.

2. Observer Feedback (15-20 minutes) Commendations (Start with Strengths)

items: Specific examples of good practice that the observer saw
Tied to rubric indicators

Example: "You used wait time after asking questions. This gave all students time to form an answer. I saw at least 5 seconds of silence after each question. Research shows this is best practice for deeper thinking. This matches Distinguished performance in the 'Uses Questioning and Discussion Techniques' indicator."
1-2 specific, practical suggestions (too many can overwhelm the teacher)
Tied to rubric indicators
Evidence-based, not opinion-based

Example: "To make the lesson more challenging and build higher-order thinking, try asking more 'why' and 'how' questions, not mainly 'what' questions. During the lesson, I noted that about 80% of the questions were recall-level (remembering facts). Adding analysis and evaluation questions would move your practice toward Proficient/Distinguished in the Questioning indicator."
Say "I noticed..." instead of "You should..."
Refer to specific moments in the lesson
Avoid educational jargon (special technical words). Be clear and concrete
Give an honest balance of praise and areas for growth (do not invent false praise)
Together, set 1-2 professional growth goals for the next observation or term
Goals should be SMART (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound)

Example Goal: "By the next observation in January, I will use at least 3 higher-order thinking questions in each lesson. These are questions at the analyze, evaluate and create levels of Bloom's Taxonomy. I will also use a wait time of at least 5 seconds after each question."
The teacher agrees to try specific strategies
Professional development opportunities (DTP webinars, Cambridge PD, peer observation)
Teaching resources (lesson plan examples, articles, videos)
Coaching or mentoring if needed
A written observation report (commendations, recommendations, goals) is shared with the teacher within 1 week
The teacher signs to confirm they received the report. The signature does not mean the teacher agrees with it.
The report is stored in the teacher's professional file in EduNav
The teacher may add a written response if they wish
Supportive and collaborative, not punitive
Recognize that teaching is complex. No one expects perfection
Growth mindset: "What you're working on" not "what you're bad at"
Celebrate progress and effort

content.text:
When Used: When a teacher's observation ratings are repeatedly Basic (Level 2) or Unsatisfactory (Level 1). It is also used when a new teacher needs intensive support.

Purpose: Give focused, structured support through a coaching cycle. This helps teachers improve specific areas of their practice.

Coaching Cycle Process (6-12 weeks):

Step 1: Goal Setting Meeting
content.title: 7.4.4 Coaching Cycle for Improvement

items.text: Identify 1-2 specific, measurable goals based on observation data
items: Example: "Increase student participation from 40% to 70% of class by end of term"
Root cause analysis: Why is this area difficult? (skill gap, knowledge gap, resources, student behavior or other factors)
Define success criteria: What will improvement look like?
The coach and the teacher plan lessons together. The coach is the HOD (Head of Department), the Academic Coordinator or an experienced peer
The coach models (shows) the strategies, gives resources and discusses expected challenges
The teacher practices explaining the new strategy to build confidence

items.text: Option A: The coach teaches the lesson while the teacher observes (modeling)
items: The teacher takes notes on the specific strategies the coach uses
Talk about the lesson (debrief) right after it: What did you notice? What questions do you have?

items.text: Option B: The coach and the teacher co-teach (gradual release)
items: The coach leads the difficult part. The teacher observes and helps
In the next lesson, the roles reverse. The teacher leads and the coach supports
The coach observes the teacher using the strategy in the teacher's own class

items.text: A quick debrief right after the lesson (5-10 minutes):
items: What went well? What was challenging?
What will you adjust next time?
Feedback is formative and focuses on growth. It is not used to evaluate the teacher for appraisal
The teacher keeps practicing the strategy alone in later lessons
The teacher reflects in a journal or with structured reflection prompts
The teacher may video-record themselves (optional) for self-assessment
A formal observation checks progress toward the goal (after 6-12 weeks of coaching)
Celebrate growth and improvement
Set the next goal if needed. If the teacher is now proficient, they move back to the standard observation cycle
Weekly check-ins (15-30 minutes) during active coaching phase
Monthly observations during coaching cycle
More intensive support (daily or every other day) for teachers who urgently need it
Coaching log with dates, focus areas, strategies tried, and progress notes
Stored confidentially. It is used to plan support, not to punish the teacher through evaluation

content.text: Mindset: Coaching is there to support, not to punish. The goal is to help every teacher reach Proficient performance. Struggling does not mean failing. It means the teacher needs more focused support. Teachers who need intensive support may also be referred to the DTP (Development of Teaching Proficiency) program. See Section 4.4 for DTP details.
Purpose: Structured support for a teacher rated Basic (Level 2) in two appraisals in a row, or Unsatisfactory (Level 1) in one appraisal. PIP (Performance Improvement Plan) Process:
content.title: 7.4.5 Performance Improvement Plans (PIPs)

items: Trigger: Two Basic ratings in a row OR one Unsatisfactory rating
Duration: usually 6-12 weeks (see 12.11)
Written improvement plan with SMART goals
Weekly coaching sessions with HOD/Academic Coordinator
Formal observations every two weeks, with written feedback
Access to targeted PD (DTP workshops, peer mentoring)
Mid-term review checkpoint
Improved to Proficient → The teacher leaves the PIP and continues the normal appraisal cycle
Still Basic → Extend PIP one more term
Still Unsatisfactory → Recommend that the contract is not renewed (following Indonesian labor law)
Documentation: All PIP records are stored in EduNav and in the teacher's personnel file.

content.text: See Section 12 (Staff Lifecycle) for the full Capability Procedure and its HR implications.
Purpose: Build self-awareness by analyzing your own teaching. Process:
content.title: 7.4.6 Video Self-Reflection

items: The teacher records a 15-20 minute part of their lesson (focusing on a specific skill)
Watch the video alone or with a mentor, using the observation rubric
Identify: 1 strength, 1 area for growth, 1 concrete action to try next time
Optional: Share clips in the PLC (Professional Learning Community) to analyze them together

content.text: Privacy: Videos are stored securely. They are used only for the teacher's own development (not for appraisal).
When Feedback is Met with Resistance:
content.title: 7.4.7 Navigating Difficult Feedback Conversations

steps: Listen First: "Tell me more about your perspective."
Use Evidence: "I observed X happening. What were you trying to achieve?"
Avoid Judgment: "This strategy didn't engage students" (not "You're a bad teacher")
Focus on Impact: "When you called on only 3 students, 25 others weren't engaged."
Collaborative Problem-Solving: "What might we try differently next time?"

content.text: When to Escalate: If the teacher refuses feedback or does not improve after 2 coaching cycles, involve the Principal and start a PIP (see 7.4.5).

content.title: Purpose
content.text: Every teacher who is new to an Eduversal Partner School joins a structured induction program. The program runs for three semesters (~18 months). It helps new teachers settle into the school community, understand the school's culture and expectations, and teach well from day one. This clause states the policy: what the program must include and who is responsible for what. The detail for participants is in the Teacher Induction Handbook (see the cross-reference below).

content.title: Policy requirements
content.text: The following requirements are binding for all Eduversal Partner Schools:

items: Duration: three semesters (~18 months) from the hire date, for every teacher new to the school. A one-semester (~6-month) extension is available if the mentor and the school leader jointly recommend it. An Accelerated Track shortens the program to two semesters (~12 months). It is for teachers with 2+ years of verified prior teaching experience, at the school leader's discretion. (Induction Charter v1.1.)

Structure: before the teacher arrives, the school completes a preparation stage (accounts, classroom, welcome pack, colleague and mentor assignment). The program itself has five phases across three semesters: (1) Familiarization (Semester 1, weeks 1-3); (2) Foundation, with weekly mentor support (rest of Semester 1); (3) Growth, built on the eight-touch observation cycle (Semester 2); (4) the Integration Checkpoint (end of Semester 2); (5) Consolidation, with monthly coaching and peer collaboration (Semester 3). The program closes with the final formal checkpoint and the completion sign-off.

Mentorship: every new teacher has a named mentor and a named colleague. School leadership assigns both before the teacher starts. The mentor is the pedagogical (teaching) guide. The mentor is an experienced teacher (typically 3+ years at the school, with Proficient or Distinguished appraisal ratings). Where possible, the mentor is from the same department. The mentor holds active Eduversal Mentor Certification and supports no more than three mentees. The colleague gives day-to-day help with settling in and does not need to teach the same subject. If no one at the school can mentor in the same subject, the school requests a cross-school mentor through Eduversal.

Developmental boundary: induction support is developmental. Mentor observations happen monthly in months 2-9 (the Observation Spine, which meets the PIGP minimum). These observations and the Semester 2 touch cycle produce formative feedback only. They never produce appraisal scores. Once the teacher enters appraisal, a former mentor never acts as that teacher’s appraiser. The program has two formal checkpoints. The school leader runs both, and both are part of the induction system. They are the Integration Checkpoint at the end of Semester 2 and the Final Formal Evaluation at the end of Semester 3.

Realistic expectations: by the end of Year 1, new teachers are expected to reach Basic to Proficient (Level 2-3) performance on most indicators. They are then expected to strengthen that practice during Semester 3. Distinguished performance is not expected in the first year.

content.title: Roles
content.text: School leadership assigns the colleague and the mentor. It reduces the new teacher's timetable across all three semesters, with a smaller reduction each semester (20% → 10% → 5%). It protects the first-year class allocation. It leads both formal checkpoints: the Integration Checkpoint (end of Semester 2) and the Final Formal Evaluation (end of Semester 3). The mentor gives day-to-day guidance and meets the mentee regularly (weekly in the first term). The mentor also reviews lesson plans, observes monthly with developmental feedback, and connects the mentee to resources and support. The mentee takes an active part in the support provided. The mentee asks for feedback and acts on it, takes part in PLCs and professional development, and reflects regularly on their practice. Eduversal provides the DTP (Development of Teaching Proficiency) program and the Teacher Induction Handbook. Eduversal also monitors first-year support at network level.

content.title: Where the detail lives
content.text: The detail for participants is in the Teacher Induction Handbook. This includes day-by-day orientation agendas, weekly checklists, the month-by-month observation focus rotation, meeting schedules and reflection templates. All staff can read the Handbook in the hub handbook reader. The operational induction procedure is in Section 12.5, including its legal basis in Permendiknas No. 27/2010 (PIGP). The program charter and its five non-negotiables are in the Eduversal Induction Charter. This section states policy only and does not repeat that material. See also the Cambridge Mentoring Guide (2020) for mentoring strategies. See Section 7.3 for the appraisal system the new teacher will enter after induction. steps: Review previous unit results

Identify gaps to work on during teaching

content.title: 7.6.1 Lesson Plan Components

items: What students will know and be able to do by end of the lesson
Aligned to Cambridge curriculum learning objectives and/or Indonesian Capaian Pembelajaran (CP)
Clear, measurable, student-friendly language
Shown clearly in the classroom at the start of the lesson: "By the end of today, you will be able to..."
"By the end of this lesson, you will be able to describe the process of photosynthesis and explain why plants need sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide."
How students (and the teacher) will know the objectives are achieved
Can be written as "I can..." statements or rubric indicators
Helps students self-assess their progress
"I can label a diagram showing the inputs and outputs of photosynthesis."
"I can explain in my own words why plants need sunlight."
"I can write the word equation for photosynthesis correctly."

items.text: Formative Assessment: How will you check understanding during the lesson?
items: Methods: Exit tickets, whiteboard checks, questioning, observation, peer assessment, think-pair-share
Identify at least 2-3 formative assessment strategies per lesson
For end-of-unit or milestone lessons, name the summative assessment (quiz, test, project, presentation)
Formative: A thumbs up/down check after explaining each step of photosynthesis. An exit ticket asking students to draw and label a photosynthesis diagram
Summative: Common Assessment Teacher-Paced Test on plant processes (scheduled for next week)
List all the materials needed: textbook pages, handouts, manipulatives (objects students can handle), technology (projector, laptops, apps) and lab equipment
Include links to videos, websites, digital files
Note any materials to prepare before the lesson (photocopies, lab setup)
Textbook: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science, pages 45-48
Video: "Photosynthesis Explained" (YouTube, 4 min) - [link]
Materials: Colored pencils, printed plant diagrams (1 per student), chart paper for group work

content.text: 6. Lesson Sequence Break the lesson into logical phases, with a time for each: Opening (5-10 minutes)

items: Hook/Engage: Get students interested and help them recall what they already know (prior knowledge)
Examples: an interesting question, a short video, a demonstration, a real-world link, a review game
Review Prior Learning: Link to the previous lesson. Check the knowledge students need first
State Objectives and Success Criteria: Share the learning goals clearly. Make sure students know what they are working toward
Hook (3 min): Show a time-lapse video of a plant growing from a seed. Ask: "Where does a plant get the energy and materials to grow this big?"
Prior Knowledge Review (2 min): A quick recap of the last lesson on plant cell structure. "What organelle is found in plant cells but not animal cells? Why is it important?"
Share Objectives (2 min): Write the objectives on the board. Students copy them into their notebooks. Make the success criteria clear.
The teacher explains, shows and models the new content
Use visuals, examples, think-aloud to make thinking visible
Check for understanding often: "Does everyone follow?" (thumbs up/down, quick questions)
For EAL (English as an Additional Language) students: Speak clearly and at a moderate speed. Use visuals and gestures. Teach key vocabulary before the lesson

Direct Instruction (8 min): Use a diagram on the board to explain the photosynthesis process step by step. Show how to label the diagram. Think-aloud: "I know chlorophyll is important, so I'll label the chloroplast first."
Check for Understanding (2 min): Quick whiteboard check. Students draw a simple diagram that shows sunlight going into a leaf. Look around the room to see who needs re-teaching.
Students Practice with Teacher Support
Work in pairs or small groups on structured task
The teacher moves around the room, gives feedback, corrects misconceptions and asks probing questions
Scaffold as needed. Slowly hand responsibility over to the students

Pair Work (12 min): Students work with a partner to complete a partly filled-in photosynthesis diagram (a word bank is provided). The teacher moves around the room and asks: "Why do you think the arrow points from sunlight to the leaf? What does that show?"
Address Misconceptions (3 min): If several students are confused about the role of carbon dioxide, explain it again briefly with a new example.
Students work independently to apply what they learned
The teacher monitors and gives individual support as needed. The teacher notes who is mastering the content and who is struggling (this informs future teaching)

Independent Task (12 min): Students complete an exit ticket. They draw and label the photosynthesis diagram from memory. They write 2-3 sentences explaining why plants need sunlight. They use colored pencils to color-code inputs and outputs.
Summarize Key Points: Review what was learned
Check for Understanding: Exit ticket, reflection question, quick quiz, self-assessment against success criteria
Preview Next Lesson: Build interest; connect to the next learning
Summary (2 min): "Today we learned that photosynthesis is how plants make food using sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide. They produce glucose and oxygen."
Exit Ticket (collected)
Preview (1 min): "Tomorrow we'll explore why photosynthesis is important for all life on Earth, including us!"

content.text: 7. Differentiation How will you support diverse learners?

items: Struggling Students: Scaffolding strategies (graphic organizers, sentence frames, modified tasks, re-teaching in small groups, peer support, extra time)
Advanced Students: Extension activities (deeper questions, independent research, enrichment projects, leadership roles such as peer tutoring)
EAL Students: Language support strategies (teaching vocabulary before the lesson, visuals, simplified language, use of L1 (the student's first language) when appropriate, sentence frames)
SEN Students: Accommodations from the IEP (Individual Education Plan), such as preferential seating, assistive technology, a reduced amount of work and alternative formats
Struggling: Give a word bank for labeling the diagram. Offer a partly completed diagram as a scaffold. Pair the student with a strong peer
Advanced: Challenge students to research photosynthesis in extreme environments (desert, underwater plants). Ask them to explain how adaptations work
EAL: Teach the key vocabulary (photosynthesis, chlorophyll, glucose, oxygen) before the lesson, with visuals and gestures. Give a diagram template in simplified language
SEN: A student with dyslexia gets a digital copy of the notes to use with text-to-speech, and extended time for the exit ticket
What went well? (Be specific: which activities, strategies, moments?)
What didn't work as planned? Why? (Student confusion, timing issues, behavior problems, unclear instructions?)
What will you do differently next time? (Concrete changes)

items.text: Student Learning Evidence: Did students meet objectives? How do you know? (Use formative assessment data)
items: Example: "12 out of 18 students correctly labeled all parts of photosynthesis diagram on exit ticket. 6 students still confused about role of chlorophyll—will re-teach in small group tomorrow."
Find patterns in your teaching practice over time
Use evidence, not just gut feelings, to improve future lessons
Set professional growth goals based on reflection
Record progress for appraisal and professional development

Create teams of teachers who work together to improve student learning. They do this through inquiry, data analysis, shared practice and solving problems together. PLCs (Professional Learning Communities) are the main way to deliver job-embedded professional development in Eduversal Partner Schools.
content.title: Purpose

content.text: PLC Composition: Schools can organize PLCs in different ways, depending on school size, structure and focus:
content.title: 7.7.1 PLC Structure

items.text: Subject-Based PLCs: Teachers of the same subject across grades (all Math teachers, all Science teachers, all English teachers)
items: Best for: Curriculum alignment, vertical articulation, subject-specific teaching methods, exam preparation strategies

items.text: Grade-Level PLCs: Teachers of the same grade across subjects (all Grade 8 teachers)
items: Best for: Student-centered discussions, cross-curricular integration, consistent behavior management, grade-level initiatives

items.text: Vertical PLCs: Teachers across grade levels for the same subject (Grades 7-9 Math teachers, or Grades 10-12 Science teachers)
items: Best for: Making sure skills progress, alignment with Cambridge Checkpoint/IGCSE/A-Level expectations, finding gaps in the curriculum

items.text: Special Focus PLCs: Temporary PLCs formed around specific initiative (EAL strategies PLC, STEAM integration PLC, Assessment Design PLC)
items: Best for: Targeted improvement in one specific area; these PLCs usually meet for one term or semester
All teachers take part in at least one PLC
PLC size: Ideally 4-8 members for productive discussion (larger groups can be split)
Membership stays the same for the year to build trust and continuity
Frequency: Decided by school leadership; usually every two weeks or monthly
Duration: 60-90 minutes per meeting
Scheduled: During the school day (e.g., common planning period, late-start days) or right after school
Non-negotiable: PLC time is protected; meetings are not canceled for other activities
Typically HOD or experienced teacher
PLC leadership can rotate so that more teachers build leadership capacity
Role: Set the agenda, keep the discussion focused, make sure every voice is heard, manage time, record decisions
Shared Responsibility: All members contribute; the PLC is collaborative, not top-down

content.text: PLCs in Eduversal schools use the Professional Learning Community model developed by Richard DuFour. It centers on four critical questions that drive continuous improvement: Question 1: What do we want students to learn?
content.title: 7.7.2 DuFour's Four Critical Questions

items: Review learning standards (Cambridge curriculum objectives, Indonesian Capaian Pembelajaran)
Make clear the essential knowledge and skills (what is most important vs. what is nice-to-know)
Develop a shared understanding of "proficiency" (what does mastery look like?)

Grade 9 IGCSE Math PLC: "For quadratic equations unit, students must be able to solve by factoring, completing the square, and using quadratic formula. They must also interpret solutions in real-world contexts. Let's agree that 'proficient' means correctly solving at least 7 out of 10 problems and explaining method choice."

content.text: Question 2: How will we know if they've learned it?

items: Design common assessments (all teachers in the PLC give the same or an equivalent assessment)
Agree on rubrics, scoring criteria, and standards for success
Calibrate scoring (moderation): Score sample student work together so that scoring is consistent

Grade 9 Math PLC creates a common end-of-unit test on quadratic equations. Each teacher brings 3 sample student solutions. The PLC scores them together, discusses borderline cases and agrees on exemplars for each performance level (Below Basic, Basic, Proficient, Advanced).

content.text: Question 3: What will we do if they haven't learned it?

items: Plan interventions and re-teaching strategies for students who do not master the content
Differentiate based on student needs (small group instruction, tutoring, modified tasks, peer support)
Monitor whether interventions work; adjust them if they are not working

After the common assessment, 12 students in the PLC's classes scored Below Basic on quadratic equations. The PLC plans these actions: (1) A small-group re-teaching session during lunch or after school, focused on factoring misconceptions. (2) Peer tutoring that pairs strong students with struggling students for homework support. (3) Re-assess after 1 week with a parallel test to check growth.

content.text: Question 4: What will we do if they already know it?

items: Plan extensions, enrichment and acceleration for students who have already mastered the content
Challenge advanced students with deeper applications, independent projects, leadership opportunities

For 6 students who scored Advanced on quadratics, the PLC plans the following. First, an enrichment project researching real-world applications of quadratics (projectile motion, architecture). Second, a challenge to derive the quadratic formula algebraically. Third, a chance to peer-tutor struggling students, which strengthens their own mastery through teaching.
Quick round: Each member shares one success or challenge since the last meeting
Builds relationships and shared awareness of what is happening in classrooms
content.title: 7.7.3 PLC Meeting Protocol

items: Revisit PLC agreements (start and end on time, everyone takes part, assume positive intent, focus on evidence not opinions, keep student data confidential)
Norms are posted where everyone can see them, or reviewed aloud

content.text: 3. Analyze Student Data (20-30 minutes) (Heart of PLC Work)

items: Review results from common assessment, formative assessment, or recent unit
Which students/groups mastered objectives? Which didn't?
What questions or concepts were most difficult? Most successful?
Are there trends by class, teacher or student subgroup (EAL, SEN, gender)?
Why did students struggle with this concept? (Missing prerequisite skills, unclear instruction, a poorly designed assessment, not enough practice time, other factors)
Why did this strategy work well? (Can we replicate it?)
Display student work samples (anonymized)
Use data charts (% of students proficient by class/teacher)
Focus on evidence, not assumptions: "I noticed students confused 'x' with variable vs. multiplication sign" (evidence) not "Students don't pay attention" (assumption)

content.text: 4. Plan Action (20-30 minutes) Based on the data analysis, the PLC decides on the next teaching steps:

items: Who needs extra support? What specific skills do they need?
What intervention strategies will we use? When? Who will deliver?
How will we progress-monitor?
Based on what worked and what did not, what will we change in the next unit's lessons?
Do we need more time on a concept? Different examples? More practice?
Share successful strategies: "When I used a real-world example of loans for teaching quadratics, students were much more engaged. Here's the activity..."
Agree to try a strategy together and report back at the next meeting

content.text: 5. Set Goals and Next Steps (10 minutes)

items: Commit to Actions: Each teacher commits to trying a specific strategy or intervention before the next meeting
Plan Next Common Assessment: What will we assess next? When? Who will draft it?
Assign Roles for Next Meeting: Facilitator, note-taker, timekeeper (rotate these roles to build leadership capacity)
Set Agenda Topics: What do we need to discuss next time?
What did we accomplish today?
What questions remain?
How well is our PLC working? (Are norms being followed? Do we need to change anything?)

content.text: PLC Norms (Agreements for How We Work Together): PLCs work best when members agree on norms for working together. Common norms:
content.title: 7.7.4 PLC Norms and Evidence

items: Focus on Learning: Keep student learning at the center of all discussions (not adult preferences or convenience)
Collaborate, Don't Compete: Share strategies openly; teaching is not a competition
Use Data and Evidence: Base decisions on student work, assessment results and observation evidence (not on hunches or anecdotes alone)
Be Respectful: Critique ideas, not people; assume positive intent; value diverse perspectives
Take Action: PLCs lead to changes in practice; discussions must result in concrete next steps
Maintain Confidentiality: Student data discussed in the PLC stays in the PLC; do not gossip about students or colleagues
Honor Time: Start and end on time; stay focused on the agenda; side conversations can happen after the meeting
Attend regularly and take an active part (PLC attendance is mandatory unless excused)
Come prepared: Bring the student work, data and materials needed for the discussion
Carry out agreed strategies: Try what the PLC decides to try; report back on the results
Contribute ideas: Do not just listen; share your insights, questions and strategies
Be open to feedback and change: Be willing to examine and improve your practice

content.text: Evidence of Effective PLCs (Artifacts for Accreditation and Quality Assurance): Documentation shows that PLCs are working as intended:

items: PLC Meeting Agendas and Notes: A record of discussions, decisions and action items (one member is the note-taker at each meeting)
Common Assessments Developed by PLC: Tests, quizzes, rubrics and projects that the PLC designs together
Student Work Samples Analyzed: Anonymized samples with PLC notes that show the analysis
Data Charts/Graphs: Charts or graphs of student performance data that the PLC reviewed
Intervention Plans: Written strategies to support students who are struggling, and data that tracks their progress

items.text: Evidence of Impact: Data from before and after PLC-designed interventions that shows improvement
items: Example: "The PLC decided to add more visual supports for EAL students in Science. On the next assessment, the share of EAL students scoring Proficient rose from 45% to 68%."

content.text:
Storage: PLC records are kept in a shared folder that school leadership and accreditation teams can open.

This shows a culture of working together and continuous improvement.

Process:

items: The observer and the observee agree on a focus area (e.g., "questioning techniques")
The observee shares the lesson plan and context
The observer takes notes on the agreed focus area
Not an evaluation (no scoring, just learning)
Observee reflects first: "How did it go?"
Observer shares "I noticed..." observations (not judgments)
Collaborative discussion: "What might we try in our own practice?"

Frequency: At least 2 peer observations per term (1 as observer, 1 as observee)

Documentation: A short reflection log (What did I learn? What will I try?), kept in the teacher's PD portfolio.
Purpose: Use the expertise of more than one teacher to improve student learning. Common Co-Teaching Models:
content.title: 7.7.6 Co-Teaching Models and Collaboration

steps: Team Teaching: Both teachers lead the lesson together (ideal for STEAM and cross-curricular units)
Station Teaching: Divide the class into groups; each teacher leads a station
Parallel Teaching: Split the class in half; both teachers teach the same content (this lowers the number of students per teacher)
One Teach, One Support: One teacher leads; the other moves around the room to help individual students (use sparingly)
Shared lesson planning time (at least 30 minutes per week)
Clearly defined roles for each lesson
Shared assessment and grading
Regular debrief: "What worked? What do we adjust?"
English and Indonesian language teachers co-teach reading comprehension
Science and STEAM teachers co-teach a design thinking project
A classroom teacher and an SEN (special educational needs) teacher co-teach a differentiated math lesson

content.text: Purpose: Enable teachers to study and improve their own practice in a planned, systematic way. Action Research Cycle:
content.title: 7.7.7 Action Research for Professional Growth

steps: Identify a Problem of Practice: "My Year 9 students struggle with persuasive writing."
Research & Plan: Read the research and design an intervention (e.g., a peer review protocol)
Implement: Try the intervention for 4-6 weeks
Collect Data: Student work samples, surveys and assessment results
Analyze & Reflect: Did it work? Why/why not?
Share Findings: Present to the PLC or at a school PD day

content.text: Support: Teachers who do action research may present their findings at the Eduversal Annual PD Conference.
Beyond Surveys: Involving Students in Teacher Growth
content.title: 7.7.8 Amplifying Student Voice

steps: Exit Tickets with Teaching Feedback: "One thing that helped me learn today:" + "One thing that confused me:"
Student Focus Groups: 4-6 students meet with the teacher every quarter to discuss "What helps you learn best in this class?"
Student-Led Conferences: Students present their learning progress to parents (the teacher guides the process)

content.text: Bring Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts, and Mathematics together across the curriculum. This builds creativity, critical thinking, collaboration, and real-world problem-solving skills. STEAM education prepares students for 21st-century challenges and careers. It also aligns with the Cambridge curriculum and Indonesian educational goals (Profil Pelajar Pancasila).
content.title: Purpose

content.text: STEAM Definition: STEAM is a learning approach that connects Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts, and Mathematics. Students use it to solve real-world problems in creative, hands-on ways. It breaks down the walls between traditional subjects. Students see how the subjects connect and apply their knowledge in real situations. Purpose of STEAM Education:

steps: Critical Thinking and Problem-Solving STEAM helps students approach challenges step by step, using evidence-based reasoning and experiments. In hands-on projects like designing a sustainable bridge or programming a robot, students learn to analyze data and test hypotheses. They improve their solutions through repeated attempts and build resilience. These skills are essential for dealing with complex real-world issues.

Interdisciplinary Knowledge STEAM mixes several subjects, so it breaks down the walls between them. Students see how professionals in fields like architecture, game design, or environmental science use different subjects. They use math for calculations, art for appearance, science to understand systems, and engineering to make things work. This leads to clear understanding and new, creative results.

Creativity and Collaboration STEAM uses artistic elements to spark imagination, and group activities build teamwork and communication. Students might work together on a multimedia project, such as an animated story about environmental science. This builds their ability to brainstorm, share feedback and improve work as a group. These skills are vital in modern workplaces. 4. 21st-Century Skills Technology is changing fast. STEAM gives learners skills like digital literacy, adaptability, and innovation. It turns students from passive users of technology into active creators. This prepares them for careers in new fields such as AI, renewable energy, robotics, and creative industries. STEAM Across K-12: STEAM has an important role at all grade levels and adapts to students' stage of development:

items: Primary (Grades 1-6): Exploration and curiosity through hands-on activities (building simple machines, coding with Scratch Jr., art-science integration)
Lower Secondary (Grades 7-8): Foundational skills and creativity (LEGO robotics, basic coding, design thinking projects)
IGCSE (Grades 9-10): Applied STEAM and analytical skills (VEX robotics, web development, engineering design challenges, competition preparation)
A-Level (Grades 11-12): Advanced specialization and competition-level projects (Arduino robotics, machine learning, CAD design, research projects for international competitions)
content.title: 7.8.1 What is STEAM Education?

content.text: Eduversal Partner Schools deliver STEAM in three phases that support each other: Phase 1: Weekly Lessons (During Regular School Hours)
content.title: 7.8.2 STEAM Implementation Framework

items: Integration: a protected weekly two-period EduSTEAM lesson delivers the EduSTEAM Annual Plan. STEAM concepts are also built into regular subject lessons (Science, Math, IT, Art, Design & Technology classes)
Frequency: Ongoing throughout academic year
Science: Do experiments using the scientific method; collect and analyze data
Math: Solve real-world problems using mathematical modeling
Art: Create visual representations of scientific concepts or mathematical patterns
Technology: Use coding to simulate scientific phenomena

content.text: Phase 2: After-School Programs (one 2-hour session per week, 12 weeks per semester)

items: Purpose: More time for hands-on projects, deeper exploration and building skills
Target: Students who want to do intensive STEAM work beyond the classroom
Activities: Robotics clubs, coding workshops, maker activities, competition teams
Duration: One academic term or a full year

content.text: Phase 3: Weekend Intensive Programs (6 weekends per term, 4 hours per session)

items: Purpose: In-depth STEAM experiences; focused skill-building; competition preparation
Structure: Saturday or Sunday sessions with specialized tracks
Target: Motivated students preparing for national/international STEAM competitions
Tracks (students select one):

steps: Interdisciplinary Projects
Robotics
Coding
Design & Modeling
Competition Preparation

content.text: Integration Strategies: Project-Based Learning (PBL) STEAM fits naturally with PBL. Students work on long, real-world projects that need them to use several subjects:
content.title: 7.8.3 Teaching STEAM Across the Curriculum

items: Science: Research renewable energy sources, environmental impact
Math: Calculate costs, scale drawings
Technology: Use CAD software to design city infrastructure; create digital presentations
Engineering: Build physical model with sustainable features (solar panels, green spaces, water recycling)
Arts: Design an attractive city layout; create marketing materials to "sell" the sustainable city concept

content.text: Real-World Problem-Solving Connect learning to issues students care about or see in their communities:

items: Example Topics: Plastic pollution in Indonesian waters, clean water access, renewable energy for rural communities, food waste reduction
Science: Analyze water quality data; understand contamination sources
Math: Calculate filtration rates; do a cost-benefit analysis of solutions
Technology: Design apps to track water quality or teach the community
Engineering: Build water filtration systems using local materials
Arts: Create awareness campaigns with posters, videos, infographics

content.text: Inquiry-Based Learning Start with strong questions that make students investigate and discover:

items: How can we reduce our school's carbon footprint?
What makes a bridge strong and stable?
How can technology help solve food security challenges in Indonesia?
How does art communicate scientific concepts?

content.text: Design Thinking Process Teach students the repeating, step-by-step design process that engineers and innovators use:

steps: Empathize: Understand the problem and user needs
Define: State clearly the problem to solve
Ideate: Brainstorm multiple possible solutions
Prototype: Build quick, testable models
Test: Collect feedback; find out what works and what doesn't
Iterate: Improve the design based on testing; repeat the cycle

content.text: Example: Grade 10 students use design thinking to create assistive devices for people with disabilities Subject-Specific STEAM Integration Examples: Science Classes

items: Include engineering challenges (build a device to protect an egg dropped from 3 meters)
Use technology for data collection and visualization (sensors, Excel/Google Sheets, graphing software)
Connect to arts through scientific illustration, models, infographics
Apply math to real-world contexts (architecture, sports analytics, financial planning, coding)
Use technology for mathematical modeling and simulations
Explore mathematical patterns in nature and art (fractals, golden ratio, tessellations)
Research STEAM topics and communicate findings through writing
Analyze how STEM concepts are portrayed in literature and media
Create multimedia presentations combining text, visuals, and technology
Explore where art and science meet (color theory and light, perspective and geometry)
Use technology for digital art creation (graphic design, animation, 3D modeling)
Design functional and beautiful objects (form follows function in industrial design)
Research Indonesian scientists, engineers, and innovators
Document traditional Indonesian technology and innovations (batik, shipbuilding, irrigation systems)
Connect Profil Pelajar Pancasila (P5) dimensions to STEAM values

content.text: Teacher Collaboration for STEAM Good STEAM teaching works best when teachers from different subjects work together. Schools support this through: Joint Planning Sessions

items.text: Schedule regular co-planning time for teachers from different subjects
items: Example: Science, Math, Art, and Technology teachers plan an integrated unit on "Sustainable Architecture"
Agree on shared learning outcomes, assessment, and timeline

items.text: Team-teach STEAM lessons with expertise from multiple disciplines
items: Example: A Math teacher and an Art teacher co-teach a lesson on geometric patterns in Islamic art and architecture

content.text: The SAMR Model (Ruben Puentedura) is a framework for judging how technology is used in lessons. Level 1: Substitution (Technology replaces a traditional tool, with no change in what the tool does)
content.title: 7.9.1 SAMR Model for Technology Integration

items: Example: Students type an essay in Google Docs instead of writing it by hand
Still useful (easier editing, spell-check), but it does not transform learning

content.text: Level 2: Augmentation (Technology replaces a tool and adds a useful improvement)

items: Example: Students work together in real time on a shared Google Doc. The teacher adds comments. The version history is saved.

items: Example: Students create a multimedia presentation that combines text, images, embedded videos and links to sources

items: Example: Students in Indonesia work with students in Kenya by video conference. Together they design solutions to clean water problems. They share data in real time and create a digital documentary together.
Completely new learning experience enabled by technology

content.text:
UDL (Universal Design for Learning) Principles: Build flexibility into learning experiences from the start. This reduces the need for individual accommodations.

Principle 1: Multiple Means of Representation (How Content is Presented)
content.title: 7.10.1 Universal Design for Learning (UDL)

items.text: Present information in several formats: text, audio, video, diagrams, hands-on activities
items: Example: Teach photosynthesis through a lecture, a video, a diagram, a physical model and reading
Helps EAL students, students who have difficulty processing what they see or hear, and students with different learning preferences

content.text: Principle 2: Multiple Means of Action and Expression (How Students Demonstrate Learning)

items.text: Offer choices in how students show what they know: written, oral, visual, digital, performance
items: Example: Students can show their understanding of a novel through an essay, presentation, video, graphic novel or podcast
Helps students with writing difficulties, EAL students, and students who are strongest in other forms of expression

content.text: Principle 3: Multiple Means of Engagement (How Students are Motivated)

items: Provide choices in topics, activities, difficulty levels
Connect to students' interests and cultures
Example: Math problem-solving where students choose context (sports, cooking, business, engineering)
Helps all students by making learning more relevant and giving them more independence

items.text: Tiered Tasks: All students work toward the same objective, but at different levels of complexity
items: Example: All students analyze persuasive techniques. Tier 1 identifies basic techniques in a simple text. Tier 3 judges how well several techniques work in a complex text.

items.text: Compacting: Assess students before teaching. Students who already know the content skip the review and work on extension tasks.
items: Example: A student who masters fractions quickly moves on to an enrichment project. The project applies fractions to real-world contexts.

Flexible Grouping: Change groups to suit the task. Use similar-level (homogeneous) groups for targeted teaching, mixed (heterogeneous) groups for peer learning, interest-based groups or random groups.

items.text: Learning Stations/Centers: Students move through a set of activities. Each activity works on the same objective in a different way.
items: Station 1: Teacher-led small group instruction
Station 2: Collaborative practice task
Station 3: Independent digital practice
Station 4: Hands-on exploration or game
Varied Pacing: Give more time to students who need it. Give extension tasks to fast finishers. These are deeper or broader challenges, not just "more work".
Choice Boards: Give students a menu of ways to show mastery (see UDL Principle 2)

items.text: Tiered Assessments: All versions assess the same standards, but with different levels of scaffolding or complexity
items: Example: All students write an argumentative essay. Struggling writers receive a graphic organizer and sentence frames. Advanced writers are required to address counterarguments.

subsections.title: Universal Design for Learning (UDL) in Lesson Planning

content.text: Give teachers full guidance on building Universal Design for Learning (UDL) principles into daily lesson planning. The aim is to turn the theory of inclusive teaching into practical classroom strategies. UDL is a shift from reacting with accommodations to planning ahead in the design. It makes sure all students can access, engage with and show mastery of curriculum content from the start. This includes EAL learners, students with SEN, gifted learners and students from different cultural backgrounds.

What UDL Looks Like in a Single Lesson Universal Design for Learning is not an extra layer added to existing lesson plans. It is a basic approach to designing teaching. It plans for differences between learners from the planning stage. In a 40-80 minute lesson, UDL principles show up in: Before the Lesson:
content.title: UDL in Daily Teaching Practice

items: Planning for Variability: The teacher thinks ahead about different student needs (language level, prior knowledge, learning preferences, attention span). The teacher builds options into the lesson from the start
Resource Preparation: Multiple formats are ready before the lesson (visual slides with little text, audio recordings, manipulatives, digital interactive tools, printed graphic organizers)
Flexible Grouping Strategies: The teacher plans whole-class, small-group, partner and independent work. The choice depends on the learning objectives and student needs
Multiple Entry Points: The teacher presents content in several ways at the same time (teacher explanation + visual diagram + physical demonstration + written summary)
Student Choice: Students choose from a set of options how to practice skills or show their understanding

Ongoing Adjustment: The teacher watches how engaged students are and how well they understand. During the lesson, the teacher changes the pace, explains again with different examples, or gives extra scaffolding
Varied Assessment Methods: Students show their learning through written responses, oral explanations, drawings, models or digital presentations. All of these assess the same learning objectives
Reflection and Iteration: The teacher reviews which UDL strategies worked best for which students. The teacher then improves the approach for the next lessons

content.text: UDL adds to the lesson planning expectations in Section 7.6. It does not replace them. The core components remain: Key Distinction: Traditional differentiation often means creating separate tasks for different groups (tiered activities). UDL gives multiple options to all students. Students choose for themselves, and this removes the stigma attached to "different" work.
content.title: Connection to Existing Lesson Planning Framework
How UDL Enhances Each Lesson Plan Component
rows: Objectives written at multiple complexity levels; same destination, different pathways
Criteria expressed in multiple formats (written checklist, visual rubric, exemplars)
Multiple means for students to show mastery (written, oral, visual, performance-based)
Different types of resources (text, video, audio, manipulatives, digital simulations), prepared before the lesson
Each phase includes multiple options for representation, engagement, and expression
Proactive design reduces need for reactive individual modifications

content.text: UDL directly supports multiple indicators in the Eduversal Teacher Appraisal System (Section 7.3): Domain 2a: Planning and Organization
content.title: How UDL Enhances Teaching Quality Standards

items: Indicator: "Designs coherent instruction" → UDL helps the lesson flow smoothly for students with different learning needs
Indicator: "Demonstrates knowledge of students" → UDL planning needs a deep understanding of how learners differ
Indicator: "Manages classroom procedures effectively" → UDL options reduce behavior problems caused by frustration or boredom
Indicator: "Organizes physical space to support learning" → UDL classrooms have flexible seating, accessible materials and different learning zones
Indicator: "Uses varied questioning and discussion techniques" → UDL encourages students to answer in several formats, not just spoken answers
Indicator: "Engages students in active learning" → UDL options increase engagement by making learning relevant and giving students autonomy
Indicator: "Demonstrates flexibility and responsiveness" → A UDL mindset prepares teachers to change their plan in response to student needs

Give quick, just-in-time re-teaching to small groups who are struggling with a specific concept
Offer extension for advanced learners: "Can you explain why plants can't do photosynthesis in the dark?"
content.title: Lesson Phase 3: GUIDED PRACTICE (10-15 minutes)

items: Quick check: "Hold up your diagram. Show me where sunlight enters the process" (visual response, no writing pressure)
Exit slip options: (1) Draw and label diagram, OR (2) Write 3 sentences explaining process, OR (3) Record 30-second audio explanation

content.text: Objective: Students use their learning on their own; the teacher assesses each student's mastery Self-Assessment Prompt (UDL-Aligned):

content.title: Lesson Phase 4: Independent Practice — UDL Principles in Practice
rows: - Student autonomy - Self-paced work - Connect to real-world

- Students choose ONE task to complete independently: (1) Complete exit ticket diagram (2) Write letter to a friend explaining photosynthesis (3) Research one plant that does photosynthesis in extreme environment (desert cactus, underwater plant) and create infographic (4) Design a poster: "Why Photosynthesis Matters for Indonesia"
- Resources available in multiple formats - Provide tools and references

- Textbook pages available (printed and digital) - Video tutorial available for students who need to review - Visual reference chart on wall - Vocabulary word wall - Access to tablets/laptops if needed
- Variety of ways to show mastery - Differentiated by product, not content
- All students show understanding of photosynthesis (same standard), but through different products - Assessment focuses on content knowledge, not format

items.text: Students reflect using success criteria checklist:
items: ☐ I can identify the inputs of photosynthesis (sunlight, water, CO₂)
☐ I can identify the outputs of photosynthesis (glucose, oxygen)
☐ I can explain why plants need sunlight
☐ I can draw and label a photosynthesis diagram
Students circle their confidence level: 😟 Struggling | 😐 Getting there | 😊 Got it!
content.title: Lesson Phase 4: INDEPENDENT PRACTICE (10-15 minutes)

items: Watch students work on their own. Note who is mastering the objectives and who needs re-teaching
Collect evidence of learning (exit tickets, diagrams, written responses) to plan the next lesson
If large gaps continue, identify students for Tier 2 intervention (see Section 8 for the MTSS framework)

content.text: Objective: Summarize learning, reinforce key concepts, preview next lesson Post-Lesson Teacher Reflection (UDL Lens):

content.title: Lesson Phase 5: Closure / Wrap-Up — UDL Principles in Practice
rows: - Visual and verbal summary - Connecting to prior and future learning

- Teacher displays anchor chart summarizing photosynthesis - Verbal recap: "Today we learned how plants make food. Let's review the 3 things plants need and the 2 things they produce." - Preview: "Tomorrow we'll explore why photosynthesis is crucial for all life on Earth, including us!"
- Student voice in closure - Celebration of effort and progress

- Quick share: "Turn to your neighbor — what was the most interesting thing you learned today?" - Celebration: "I saw amazing collaboration and great questions today. You're becoming expert biologists!"
- Varied closure activities - Exit ticket options

- Exit Ticket Options (choose 1): (1) 3-2-1: Write 3 things you learned, 2 things you found interesting, 1 question you still have (2) Draw a quick sketch showing photosynthesis (3) Emoji reaction: How confident are you with today's content? Draw 😟 😐 😊 (4) Digital poll: Use tablet to answer multiple choice question

items: What worked? Which UDL strategies led to high engagement and understanding?
What didn't? Did any options confuse students or cause practical problems?
Student variability: Which students did well with which options? Which students still need extra support?
Next steps: What will I adjust for tomorrow's lesson based on today's data?

content.text: This section gives a full menu of UDL-aligned strategies. Teachers can choose from it when they plan each phase of a lesson. Not every strategy is used in every lesson. Teachers choose the best options for the learning objectives, student needs and available resources.
Purpose: Get attention, activate prior knowledge, show relevance, motivate learning
content.title: ENGAGEMENT Strategies for Lesson Opening/Hook
ENGAGEMENT Strategies for Lesson Opening/Hook
rows: Offer 2-3 options for how students engage with opening prompt
"Choose: Write your prediction, draw a diagram, or discuss with partner"
Connect lesson to students' lives, current events, or local context
"Yesterday, Jakarta had air quality issues. How does this relate to photosynthesis?"
Incorporate examples, images, or contexts familiar to Indonesian students
Use images of Indonesian rice terraces, local plants, traditional markets
Pose intriguing question or show surprising phenomenon
Sparks curiosity; appeals to students who love challenges
"How can a tiny seed grow into a massive tree? Where does all that matter come from?"
Students brainstorm questions about topic before instruction
"What do you wonder about plants? Write 2 questions you'd like answered today"
"Stand up. Stretch your arms like branches. Now, absorb sunlight (arms up). You're photosynthesizing!"
Short video, audio clip, animation, or interactive simulation
Appeals to visual and auditory learners
2-minute time-lapse video of plant growth with upbeat music

content.text: Purpose: Present information in multiple formats to meet different learning needs
content.title: REPRESENTATION Strategies for Content Delivery
REPRESENTATION Strategies for Content Delivery
rows: Simultaneously use visual, auditory, and kinesthetic modalities
Reaches all learners; reinforces through multiple pathways
While explaining photosynthesis, the teacher draws a diagram (visual) and explains aloud (auditory); students copy with hand gestures (kinesthetic)
Break complex content into smaller, digestible parts with pauses for processing
Reduces cognitive load; supports working memory
Teach photosynthesis in 3 mini-lessons: (1) Inputs, (2) Process inside leaf, (3) Outputs
Provide visual frameworks (concept maps, Venn diagrams, flowcharts)
Provide flowchart template showing photosynthesis steps with arrows and boxes
Teacher verbalizes thinking process while modeling skill
Makes invisible thinking visible; supports metacognition
"When I label this diagram, I ask myself: Where does sunlight enter? I'll start there..."
Relate abstract concepts to concrete, familiar ideas
Builds on prior knowledge; aids comprehension
"Photosynthesis is like cooking: ingredients (sunlight, water, CO₂) are combined to make a meal (glucose)"
Pre-teach key terms with visuals, gestures, and context
Critical for EAL learners; supports all students in accessing content
Display word wall with pictures: "Photosynthesis" (image of sun + leaf + arrow = apple)
Provide written text alongside videos or audio
Supports EAL, deaf/hard-of-hearing, and students who process better through reading
All videos shown in class have English captions turned on
Use color-coding, underlining, bold text, or verbal emphasis
Directs attention; supports students with attention challenges
"This is the MOST important part: Chlorophyll captures sunlight energy" (write in green on board)
Provide diverse examples, including familiar and novel contexts
Photosynthesis examples: trees, grass, algae, houseplants, seaweed, moss

content.text: Purpose: Let students show their learning and practice skills in different ways
content.title: ACTION & EXPRESSION Strategies for Student Activities
ACTION & EXPRESSION Strategies for Student Activities
rows: Menu of activity options (all addressing same learning goal)
Empowers student agency; removes "one size fits all" approach
"Choose 1: Write essay, create poster, record video explanation, build model, design infographic"
Change group types (whole class, small group, partners, individual) to fit the task and student needs
Accommodates social vs. independent learners; allows peer support
Sentence frames, paragraph templates, word banks, graphic organizers
Lowers barriers for EAL and struggling writers while maintaining rigor
Provide: "Photosynthesis is the process of ___. Plants need ___, ___, and ___"
Allow students to explain, present, or discuss instead of writing
Supports EAL learners who are still developing their English. Removes writing barriers when assessing content knowledge
Student explains photosynthesis to teacher/peer verbally instead of written quiz
Drawing, diagramming, creating models, photography, videography
Draw labeled diagram instead of written explanation
Use apps, websites, simulations, presentation software
Appeals to tech-savvy students; provides assistive features (text-to-speech, speech-to-text)
Create photosynthesis slideshow using Canva or Google Slides
Building models, role-playing, gestures, movement-based activities
Engages kinesthetic learners; makes abstract concepts tangible
Build 3D model of leaf showing chloroplasts, or act out photosynthesis process with peers
Silent thinking time → Partner discussion → Whole class share
Gives EAL and quieter (introverted) students time to think. Reduces the stress of having to answer in public straight away
"Think 30 seconds silently... Now tell your partner... Who wants to share with class?"
Offer multiple formats for demonstrating end-of-lesson understanding
Quick formative assessment without "one way only" constraint
Choose: Written summary, drawing, multiple-choice on tablet, verbal explanation to teacher

content.text: Technology can be a powerful support for UDL when teachers use it with a clear purpose. Below are tools commonly available in Eduversal Partner Schools: Important Notes on Technology Use:
content.title: Technology Tools that Support UDL

rows: - Post assignments with choice of submission formats - Attach videos, readings, slides for multi-modal access - Provide written instructions alongside video tutorials
Post photosynthesis assignment: "Submit diagram (photo), written explanation (Doc), OR video explanation"
- Read digital texts aloud for students with reading difficulties or EAL learners - Available in Chrome (Read Aloud extension), tablets, laptops
Student listens to textbook chapter on photosynthesis instead of reading silently
- Lets students dictate (speak) their written answers - Removes writing barriers for students with dysgraphia (difficulty with handwriting) or EAL learners still developing writing skills
Student verbally explains photosynthesis; software types their response
- Display multimedia content (videos, diagrams, simulations) - Students interact with touchscreen to label, move objects, annotate
Students come to board to drag-and-drop labels onto photosynthesis diagram
- Gamified formative assessment - Multiple-choice format removes writing barriers - Instant feedback; competitive element increases motivation
Kahoot quiz on photosynthesis vocabulary at end of lesson
- Digital collaboration board - Students post ideas via text, images, drawings, links
Students post examples of photosynthesis in real life (photos from home) on class Padlet
- Interactive science simulations - Students manipulate variables and observe outcomes - Visual and kinesthetic learning
Students adjust light intensity in PhET simulation and observe effect on photosynthesis rate
- Create visual products (posters, infographics, diagrams) - Templates provided for scaffolding
Students design infographic explaining photosynthesis using Canva template
- Students record video explanations or demonstrations - Alternative to written assessments
Student creates 1-minute video teaching photosynthesis to younger sibling
- Help EAL students understand content in their first language (L1) at first - Caution: Use it for understanding, not as a substitute for learning English
EAL student translates complex vocabulary to Indonesian to confirm understanding, then works in English

items: Equity: Make sure all students can use devices and reliable internet. Give other options to students without access at home (school library, borrowed devices, offline activities).
Purpose-Driven: Technology is a tool, not the goal. Use it only when it improves learning, not just because it is new.
Digital Citizenship: Teach responsible use, online safety, and academic integrity (see Section 7.9.3).
