content.text: Students in Eduversal Partner School classrooms are naturally very different. They differ in:

items: Academic readiness (below grade level, on grade level, above grade level)
Language level (from early-stage EAL learners to fluent English speakers)
Learning differences (SEN (Special Educational Needs), gifted, typical learners)
Cultural backgrounds (Indonesian, Arab, international)
Social and economic background (day students, boarding students; rural and urban backgrounds)

content.text: UDL gives teachers a framework to deal with these differences. Teachers do not need to create a separate lesson for each group.

content.title: How UDL Addresses Differentiation in Heterogeneous Classes

steps: Teach a standard lesson
Identify students who didn't understand
Create modified activities for students who struggle
Create extension activities for advanced students
Result: The teacher creates 3-5 different versions of the same lesson (too much work)
Anticipate variability from the start
Build multiple pathways into the lesson plan (options for all students)
All students work on the same core content and standards
Students choose suitable options themselves, or the teacher gives them suitable options
Result: One flexible lesson design that serves all learners

items: Below grade-level academic skills
Gaps in prior knowledge
Low confidence; fear of failure
Slow processing speed
Need more scaffolding (step-by-step support) and repetition

content.title: UDL Strategies for Struggling Learners
rows: Representation: Give the same content in simpler formats (audio, video, images, simplified text)
Instead of reading a long, difficult textbook chapter, students watch a video, listen to an audio summary and look at diagrams with notes
Action & Expression: Flexible pacing; extra time; less work, but at the same level of challenge
Complete 5 labels on the photosynthesis diagram instead of 10; OR get extra time to complete all 10
Engagement: Activate and build prior knowledge before new content
Pre-teach vocabulary and prerequisite concepts 1-2 days before main lesson
Low confidence; avoidance of hard tasks
Engagement: Offer choice; celebrate small wins; normalize mistakes
"Choose the starting point that feels right for you. Everyone starts somewhere!"
Action & Expression: Allow non-written responses; provide sentence frames; use speech-to-text
Explain photosynthesis verbally or draw diagram instead of essay

items: Do NOT lower expectations for struggling students. They must reach the same learning standards.
DO provide scaffolding (support that is removed step by step), not permanent changes to the work.
Example: All students learn the inputs and outputs of photosynthesis (the same standard). Students who struggle may use a word bank at first. Then they work toward labeling from memory.

content.title: Supporting Gifted and Advanced Students Through UDL

items: Rapid mastery of grade-level content
Deep curiosity; love of complexity and challenge
Preference for working and exploring independently
Risk of becoming bored and losing interest if the work is not challenging enough

content.title: UDL Strategies for Advanced Learners
rows: Engagement: Provide extension tasks that deepen/broaden understanding (not just "more work")
After learning the basics of photosynthesis, research photosynthesis in extreme places (Antarctic moss, desert cacti) or other pathways (C3, C4, CAM plants)
Engagement: Student-driven inquiry; choice in topics and products
Design independent research project: "Investigate one way humans are harnessing photosynthesis for renewable energy"
Representation + Action/Expression: Offer complex resources; require higher-order thinking tasks
Read a scientific research article on photosynthesis (instead of the textbook). Create a presentation that evaluates the research.
Engagement: Opportunities to mentor/tutor; leadership roles
Advanced student explains photosynthesis to struggling peer (reinforces mastery through teaching)
Action & Expression: Always have extension options ready
Early finishers choose: (1) Create a study guide for classmates, (2) Design a game or quiz on photosynthesis, (3) Free-choice extension topic

items.text: Prefer depth (exploring the same topic more deeply) over breadth (adding unrelated content)
items: Example: Don't just say "Do more problems." Say "Investigate why some plants are more efficient at photosynthesis than others."

content.text: EAL (English as an Additional Language) students are in almost every Eduversal Partner School classroom (40-70% of students). UDL naturally supports language development. UDL Strategies Particularly Effective for EAL: Balancing L1 Support with English Development:

content.title: UDL Strategies Particularly Effective for EAL Learners
rows: - Visual supports (images, diagrams, gestures, real objects or "realia") - Pre-teach vocabulary with pictures and context - Provide translations of key terms (Indonesian/Arabic glossaries) - Use simple language without making the content less challenging
Show a photosynthesis diagram with images; pre-teach "chlorophyll, glucose, carbon dioxide" with picture cards; provide a bilingual glossary

- Use the L1 (first language) to bring out what students already know - Connect to familiar cultural contexts - Give think time before speaking; use Think-Pair-Share - Pair with a bilingual peer buddy
Ask students to discuss what they know about plant growth in Indonesian/Arabic first, then switch to English

- Allow answers in L1 at first, then translate them into English - Use sentence frames for academic language - Accept drawings, diagrams and demonstrations instead of written essays - Use speech-to-text to support writing
Provide a sentence frame: "Photosynthesis is ___. Plants need ___ to survive." The student fills in the blanks, using a word bank

items: Do allow students to work through complex ideas in L1 so that they understand them
Do NOT allow students to avoid learning English completely
Goal: Use L1 as a bridge, not a crutch (something students lean on). Increase English use step by step as students' English improves.

content.text: Bringing in UDL takes time. Schools and teachers should not try to change all lessons at once. Use the following phased approach: Phase 1: Awareness and Understanding (Term 1: July-September) Goals: All teachers understand UDL principles and see examples Activities:
content.title: Timeline for Rolling Out UDL in Lesson Planning

items: 2-hour workshop introducing UDL (what, why, how)
Watch video examples of UDL lessons
Analyze sample lesson plans with UDL lens
Each PLC (Professional Learning Community) reviews one unit. It finds where teachers already use UDL strategies (often without knowing it)
Celebrate existing good practices
Teachers choose 1-2 upcoming lessons to redesign using UDL
Use UDL planning checklist (see Section 7.11.6)

content.text: Phase 2: Experimentation and Practice (Term 2-3: October-March) Goals: Teachers start to plan UDL into their lessons on purpose; they share results in PLCs Activities:

items: Teachers co-plan one UDL-enhanced lesson
One teacher teaches while others observe
Debrief: What UDL strategies worked? What was challenging?
Teachers observe colleagues who use UDL and borrow strategies that work
School leadership sets a monthly focus: "This month, try using Multiple Means of Engagement in lesson hooks"
Teachers share successes in staff meetings or on a digital bulletin board
HODs (Heads of Department) build a library of UDL resources: graphic organizer templates, choice board examples, sentence frames, digital tools

content.text: Phase 3: Refinement and Integration (Term 4: April-June + Ongoing) Goals: UDL becomes standard practice and is part of all lesson planning Activities:

items: School leadership looks for UDL in use during classroom observations (informal walkthroughs and formal appraisals)
The appraisal rubric (Section 7.3) names UDL directly in indicators such as "Demonstrates knowledge of students" and "Demonstrates flexibility and responsiveness"
Teachers submit UDL-enhanced lesson plans quarterly for the HOD/Academic Coordinator to review
Best examples shared school-wide
Annual PD (professional development) returns to UDL with new focus areas (e.g., in Year 2, a focus on assessment design for UDL)
Teacher reflections help set next year's PD priorities

Benefits: Builds expertise inside the school; fits the training to the school's context

HODs and Academic Coordinators review teachers' schemes of work (unit plans) and lesson plans from time to time. They check that UDL principles are built in.

Use this checklist:

UDL Unit Planning Quality Checklist (Use when reviewing Schemes of Work)

Review Process:

content.title: UDL Unit Planning Quality Checklist (Use when reviewing Schemes of Work)
rows: ☐ Unit includes varied entry points and hooks to spark interest ☐ Connections to real-world relevance and student interests are explicit ☐ Students have choice in topics, activities, or difficulty levels at some point ☐ Cultural relevance: Indonesian/local contexts included ☐ Opportunities for collaboration and autonomy balanced

☐ Content presented through multiple modalities (visual, auditory, kinesthetic, text) ☐ Vocabulary pre-taught for EAL students; glossaries or word walls planned ☐ Complex content chunked into smaller sections ☐ Graphic organizers and scaffolding tools included ☐ Key concepts highlighted or emphasized visually

☐ Assessments allow for multiple formats (written, oral, visual, digital, performance) ☐ Formative assessments embedded throughout unit (not just summative) ☐ Choice boards or menus of options for demonstrating mastery ☐ Scaffolds provided (sentence frames, templates, exemplars) without limiting rigor ☐ Technology tools integrated purposefully

☐ EAL strategies explicitly planned (visuals, simplified language, sentence frames) ☐ SEN accommodations referenced (based on IEPs) ☐ Strategies for struggling learners (scaffolds, modeling, reteaching opportunities) ☐ Extensions planned for advanced learners (depth, not just more work) ☐ Flexible grouping strategies outlined

☐ UDL embedded proactively (not reactive "add-on") ☐ Learning objectives remain rigorous for all students ☐ Variety of options is manageable (not overwhelming for teacher) ☐ Evidence of student voice/choice present ☐ Lesson flow is coherent and purposeful

steps: Quarterly Review: HODs review sample lesson plans from each teacher in their department
Feedback: Give written feedback that names strengths and 1-2 areas for growth
Follow-Up: Teachers submit revised lessons showing growth
Documentation: Strong UDL examples are kept as school resources. Common difficulties are addressed in PD.

content.text: Using UDL is not always easy. Below are common challenges and practical solutions:
Concern: Teachers feel overwhelmed because they need to create multiple options for every part of a lesson. Solutions:
content.title: Challenge 1: "UDL takes too much time to plan!"

items: Start Small: Don't try to use UDL in every lesson at once. Begin with one unit, then expand step by step.
Prioritize: Focus UDL work on high-stakes lessons (introducing new concepts, assessments), not on every daily routine.
Collaborate: PLCs (Professional Learning Communities) plan UDL lessons together and share out the work. Share resources across the team.
Reuse and Adapt: Once you create UDL options for one unit, you can reuse or adapt many of them for future units/years.
Quality over Quantity: Offer 2-3 meaningful choices, not 10 overwhelming options.
Mindset Shift: UDL saves time in the long run. It reduces the need for reactive interventions and for re-teaching when students don't understand the first time.

content.text: Concern: Teachers in schools with few resources worry that they lack the technology, manipulatives, or materials needed for UDL. Solutions:
content.title: Challenge 2: "I don't have enough resources or materials!"

items.text: Low-Tech UDL Works: UDL doesn't need expensive technology. Simple strategies work well:
items: Drawings instead of digital presentations
Think-Pair-Share costs nothing
Sentence frames written on paper
Real objects from the students' surroundings, used as manipulatives (hands-on learning objects)
Creative Use of Available Resources: If you have one device, let students take turns using it. If you have textbooks, use them creatively (students annotate, illustrate, create study guides).
Community Resources: Borrow materials from the school library. Ask parents for donations (magazines for collages, recyclables for building). Partner with local organizations.
Digital Resources Are Often Free: Many UDL-friendly tools cost nothing: Google Docs/Slides, YouTube educational videos, PhET simulations, Khan Academy.

content.text: Concern: Teachers are confused about the difference between traditional differentiation and UDL. They may resist "another new initiative." Clarification:
content.title: Challenge 3: "How is UDL different from differentiation? Isn't this what I already do?"

items: Reactive: Identify struggling students after the first teaching fails
Separate tasks: Create different assignments for low/average/high groups
Can be stigmatizing: Students know they're in the "slow group"
Teacher-intensive: Requires creating multiple lesson versions
Proactive: Expect variability and build flexibility into the lesson from the start
Universal options: Choices available to all students; self-selection or teacher assignment
Reduces stigma: Everyone uses the same menu of options
Teacher-efficient: One flexible design serves all

content.text: Bottom Line: If you already differentiate well, UDL will feel familiar but simpler. UDL is a change in mindset: you design for accessibility from the start instead of fixing problems afterwards.
Concern: When students have a choice, some always choose the task that needs the least effort and avoid challenging work. Solutions:
content.title: Challenge 4: "Students abuse choice; they always pick the easiest option!"

items: "Choice is a privilege that comes with responsibility. You must choose the option that will help you grow."
Teach students to self-assess: "Which option will challenge me appropriately? Not too easy, not too hard?"

items.text: Guided Choice: The teacher can direct students toward suitable options based on data:
items: "Amira, I noticed you struggled with vocabulary last unit. Today, please choose the option with word bank support."
"Ravi, you've mastered basic skills. Please choose the extension task today."

items.text: All Options Must Be Rigorous: Design the choices so that all of them lead to the same learning standard. None of them is an "easy out."
items: Example: Photosynthesis diagram (visual), written explanation (verbal), 3D model (kinesthetic)—all require understanding photosynthesis, just expressed differently.
Variety Is Key: If students always choose same option (always draw, never write), require rotation: "This week, everyone tries a format they haven't used yet."
Metacognitive Reflection: After the task, students reflect: "Did your choice help you learn? Why or why not?" This builds self-awareness over time.

content.text: Concern: Several activities happening at the same time create noise, confusion, and discipline issues. Solutions:
content.title: Challenge 5: "Class management becomes chaotic with too many options!"

items.text: Clear Procedures and Routines: Teach students how to move between options, where to find materials, and the expected noise level.
items: Practice routines early in the year until they become automatic.

items.text: Limit Simultaneous Activities: Don't run 5 different activities at once. Offer choice within structured phases:
items: Phase 1: All students do same Hook activity (whole class)
Phase 2: Students choose from 2-3 practice options (small groups)
Phase 3: All students do closure together (whole class)
Strategic Grouping: If you offer choice stations, rotate students through the stations on different days, not all at once.
Visual Timers and Signals: Use a timer to keep students on task. Use a bell or hand signal to get attention quickly.
Independent Work Systems: Train students to work independently. Then the teacher can move around and support students instead of directing them all the time.

content.text: Concern: If students show mastery in different ways (essay vs. diagram vs. presentation), how does the teacher make grading fair and consistent? Solutions:
content.title: Challenge 6: "How do I assess fairly when students complete different tasks?"

items.text: Standards-Based Assessment: Grade against learning objectives, not task format.
items: Example: All students must show understanding of photosynthesis. Whether they write an essay, draw a diagram, or create a video, assess the same things: Did they correctly identify inputs/outputs? Did they explain the process? The rubric focuses on content, not format.
Create a rubric that assesses what is learned (content mastery, critical thinking, accuracy), not how it is presented (essay structure, drawing neatness).
Example Rubric Criterion: "Accurately identifies all inputs and outputs of photosynthesis" (applies to essay, diagram, or video equally)
Moderation in PLCs: Teachers bring different student products to the PLC. They score them together to agree on what "Proficient" means.
Transparency: Share the rubric with students before the task. Then they know exactly what will be assessed, whatever format they choose.

subsections.title: Conclusion: UDL as a Teaching Mindset

content.text: Universal Design for Learning is more than a set of strategies. It is a basic change in how teachers think about learners and learning. UDL does not design lessons for an imaginary "average" student and then rush to adapt them for the students who don't fit. Instead, UDL asks teachers to expect diversity and to design flexibility from the start. Core UDL Beliefs:

steps: Variability is the norm, not the exception. Every classroom contains a beautifully diverse range of learners.
Disability is often a mismatch between the learner and the environment, not a deficit inside the learner. When we design accessible lessons, "disabilities" decrease.
Student choice and autonomy increase engagement and learning. When students have a voice in their learning journey, motivation rises sharply.
One size does not fit all, but one flexible design can fit most. Teachers don't need to create 30 individual lessons. They need one well-designed flexible lesson.

items: Year 1: Awareness and experimentation. Teachers try UDL strategies, make mistakes, learn what works.
Year 2-3: Refinement and integration. UDL becomes more natural; teachers build resource libraries.
Year 4+: Mastery and innovation. UDL comes naturally; teachers mentor others and find new ways to use it.

content.text: Impact on Students: When UDL is done well, students experience:

items: Greater access to challenging content (fewer barriers)
Increased engagement (relevance, choice, autonomy)
Deeper learning (when content is presented and practiced in multiple ways, understanding grows stronger)
Higher achievement (students show mastery through their strengths)
Improved self-efficacy (belief in their own ability: "I can learn; there are pathways for me")
Reduced frustration (fewer students fall behind or misbehave because lessons are not accessible)
More efficient (planning ahead reduces reactive interventions)
Greater creativity (UDL encourages innovation in teaching methods)
Professional satisfaction (joy of seeing all students succeed)

content.text: Final Encouragement: Using UDL is a journey, not a destination. No lesson will ever be "perfectly" UDL-aligned, and that's okay. Start small, reflect, adjust, and grow. Ask for support from colleagues, HODs (Heads of Department), and the wider Eduversal community. Remember: every step toward more inclusive, flexible lesson design helps students. Your commitment to UDL is a commitment to equity, excellence, and the belief that every student can learn.

content.title: Culturally Responsive Strategies

items: Learn students' names correctly; ask how to pronounce them
Show real interest in students' lives, cultures, and languages
Home visits or parent meetings to understand family context (when culturally appropriate)
Use the "Funds of Knowledge" approach: recognize the knowledge and skills students bring from home/community

items.text: Literature: Include Indonesian authors alongside British/American texts

items.text: History: Look at events from multiple perspectives, including Indonesian/Southeast Asian viewpoints

items.text: Science: Highlight the contributions of Indonesian and Muslim scientists
items: Example: Discuss Habibie's contributions to aerospace engineering; Al-Khwarizmi's role in mathematics
Math: Use contexts familiar to students (rupiah, local markets, Indonesian companies)
Encourage translanguaging: Use of Indonesian/Arabic for thinking and initial learning (not penalized)
Celebrate cultural and religious holidays (Idul Fitri, Idul Adha, Independence Day)
Display student work in multiple languages
Invite families to share cultural traditions
Deficit thinking: "These EAL students can't do complex work" ❌
Asset thinking: "These multilingual students are developing valuable skills; I'll provide scaffolding so they can access challenging content" ✅
Communicate the belief that all students can achieve; give them the tools and support to make it happen

content.text: Address Bias and Create Inclusive Environment

items: Check the curriculum for stereotypes or missing voices

Respond quickly to microaggressions (small, everyday insults or put-downs) or exclusionary behavior
Show respect for all cultures, religions, and identities through your own behavior

subsections.title: AI and Academic Integrity in Teaching

content.text: Handle the fast-changing world of artificial intelligence (AI) in education responsibly. Teach students to use AI ethically as a tool. At the same time, keep academic integrity and develop critical thinking skills.
content.title: Purpose

content.text: Appropriate Teacher Uses of AI: Lesson Planning and Resource Creation
content.title: 7.13.1 Teacher Use of AI

items: Generate lesson plan drafts, discussion questions, and activity ideas (always review and adapt them)
Create differentiated versions of texts or problems
Develop rubrics, assessment questions, example scenarios
Critical: Always fact-check AI output; AI can produce wrong information
Draft parent emails (personalize before sending)
Summarize meeting notes
Create data visualizations from assessment results
Explore teaching strategies for specific challenges
Generate ideas for classroom management or engagement
Practice difficult conversations (AI as role-play partner)
Never enter personally identifiable student information (information that can identify a student) into AI tools (this violates privacy)
Don't rely on AI alone; professional judgment is essential
Be open with colleagues about materials made with AI help

content.text: Educators must teach students directly about AI (what it can do, its limits, ethics, appropriate use). AI Literacy Curriculum (Integrate Across Subjects): Understanding AI Basics
content.title: 7.13.2 Teaching Students About AI

items: What is AI? How does it work (simplified)?
Types of AI: Generative (ChatGPT, DALL-E), Analytical (recommendation systems), Predictive (spam filters)
Limitations: AI does not truly understand. It can give false information with confidence ("hallucinations"). It reflects biases in its training data
Always check AI-generated information against credible sources
Recognize when AI gives answers that sound right but are wrong
Understand that AI cannot replace human creativity, critical thinking, or ethical judgment
Appropriate uses: Brainstorming, outlining, checking grammar, learning new concepts
Inappropriate uses: Submitting AI-generated work as your own, skipping the learning process, academic dishonesty
Giving credit: Cite AI use when required by assignment
Benefits: Accessibility (text-to-speech for visually impaired), efficiency, innovation
Risks: Job losses, misinformation, privacy concerns, algorithmic bias (unfair results built into AI systems)
Responsible AI development and use

content.text: School Policy on Student AI Use: The network baseline is Digital Citizenship & AI Appendix B: AI Responsible Use Policy 26-27. Under this policy, the teacher states the permitted AI level for each task. Each school aligns its local rules with it. Each school also communicates these rules to students/parents through the Student Handbook. Typical policy includes:
content.title: 7.13.3 Detecting and Addressing AI Misuse

items: Permitted Uses: Brainstorming, grammar checking, understanding concepts explained by AI tutor, generating practice problems
Prohibited Uses: Submitting AI-written essays/assignments as your own work without disclosure; using AI to complete assessments that are meant to measure individual learning
Declaration Requirement: When an assignment allows AI use, students must state how they used AI and cite it
A sudden, large improvement in the quality or complexity of the writing
Words or phrasing that do not match the student's usual work
General content with no personal voice and no examples from class
Factual errors or "hallucinations" that are common in AI (wrong dates, fake citations, information that sounds believable but is false)
Work that does not fully answer the specific requirements of the assignment
AI detectors (Turnitin, GPTZero) have limited accuracy. Use them as one piece of evidence, not as final proof
Better approach: Design assignments that are hard to misuse with AI (see below)

steps.text: Talk with the Student (be curious; do not accuse)
items: "Can you explain your thinking process for this part of your essay?"
"Tell me more about this source you cited—where did you find it?"
A student who is unable to explain their own work is a strong sign of misuse

steps: Review Evidence: Compare the work with the student's previous work and look for patterns

items: First offense: The student does the assignment again under supervision and has a discussion about academic integrity
Repeated offenses: More serious consequences (See Student Handbook - Academic Integrity Policy)

steps: Document Incident: Record it in the student's file and inform parents

content.text: Assignment Design to Reduce AI Misuse: Strategies:

items.text: Personalization: Require students to connect the work to their own experiences, observations and community
items: Example: "Write essay analyzing symbolism in Things Fall Apart and connecting themes to a current event in your own community (name specific event)."
Process-Based Assessment: Require students to submit brainstorms, outlines, drafts and reflections. AI is not able to copy a real process that happens over time
In-Class Components: Timed writing, presentations and discussions where students must explain their thinking
Specific, Unique Prompts: Avoid general essay topics that are easy to find online or to produce with AI
Oral Defense: Students present their work and answer questions about their process and choices
Multimodal: Combine written work with visual, audio, or hands-on components

subsections.title: AI Integration Policy Framework for School Leadership

content.text: Purpose This section sets out a full institutional framework for AI integration across Eduversal partner schools. It gives school leaders strategic guidance on implementation, resource allocation, professional development, data governance and quality assurance. It adds to the practical classroom guidance in Section 7.13 by covering the wider organizational and leadership side of AI adoption.

content.title: 7.14.1 Strategic Planning for AI Integration
content.text:
School leaders are responsible for developing a clear AI integration strategy. The strategy is aligned with Cambridge International standards, Indonesian regulatory requirements and the school's improvement priorities.

**Key Components of an AI Integration Plan:**

content.title: Vision and Objectives
items: Explain how AI integration supports the school's educational mission
Set specific, measurable goals for AI adoption (for example, the percentage of teachers using AI for lesson planning, or benchmarks for student AI literacy)
Align AI initiatives with existing school improvement plans and Cambridge quality standards

content.title: Priority Areas for Implementation
items: Phase 1: Teacher productivity tools (lesson planning, material creation, administrative tasks)
Phase 2: Better assessment and feedback
Phase 3: Student-facing applications and AI literacy curriculum
Phase 4: Advanced personalization and data-driven instruction

content.title: Resource Requirements
items: Infrastructure needs (reliable internet, devices, platform subscriptions)
Budget allocation for AI tools and professional development
Technical support capacity

content.title: Timeline and Milestones
items: Realistic implementation schedule with clear checkpoints
Pilot programs before full-scale rollout
Regular review points to check progress and adjust the approach

content.title: Risk Assessment
items: Identifying possible challenges (staff resistance, technical issues, academic integrity concerns)
Strategies to reduce each identified risk
Contingency plans for implementation setbacks

content.title: 7.14.2 Approved AI Tools and Platforms
content.text:
Schools must keep a carefully chosen list of approved AI tools. Each tool on the list has been checked for educational suitability, data privacy compliance and alignment with school values.

**Criteria for Tool Approval:**

content.title: Educational Value
items: A clear teaching purpose and evidence of benefit to teaching or learning
Age-appropriateness for intended users
Alignment with Cambridge curriculum objectives

content.title: Data Privacy and Security
items: Compliance with Indonesian data protection regulations (UU PDP - Undang-Undang Pelindungan Data Pribadi)
Clear data handling policies from the provider
The tool does not require users to enter information that identifies students. If such input is necessary, the tool gives strong protection
Data storage location and security measures

content.title: Reliability and Support
items: Stable platform with consistent availability
Adequate technical support from provider
Regular updates and improvement

content.title: Cost-Effectiveness
items: Reasonable pricing relative to educational benefit
Sustainable within school budget constraints
Clear licensing terms

content.text: The Eduversal network keeps a centrally approved tool list and updates it every term. Schools may propose extra tools for network review. Using non-approved tools for work that involves student information is prohibited.

content.title: Current Categories of Approved Tools
items: Generative AI assistants for teacher productivity
Assessment and quiz generation platforms
Language support tools for EAL (English as an Additional Language) students
Administrative automation tools

content.text: The specific approved tools are listed in a separate document. The office of the Eduversal Chief Academic Officer keeps this document and sends it to all partner schools.

content.title: 7.14.3 Data Governance and Privacy Protection
content.text:
Protecting student data is a key leadership responsibility. School leaders must set up and enforce strong data governance practices.

**Core Data Protection Principles:**

content.title: Data Minimization
items: Use only the minimum necessary information in any AI application
Avoid entering detailed student information when a general question is enough
Use combined (aggregate) data instead of individual records where possible

content.title: Anonymization Requirements
items: When you need AI to analyze student performance, remove or code any information that identifies students
Use class-level or cohort-level data instead of individual student data where possible
Set clear procedures for any exceptions that need identifiable data

content.title: Consent and Transparency
items: Inform parents about the AI tools used in teaching, through suitable school communications
Get the consents required by Indonesian regulations
Be open about how student data is used and protected

content.title: Secure Storage and Transmission
items: Make sure any AI-related data stored locally is properly secured
Use encrypted connections when sending sensitive information
Regularly audit data storage practices

content.title: Incident Response
items: Set clear procedures for responding to suspected data breaches
Requirements to report immediately to school leadership and Eduversal
Documentation and remediation protocols

content.title: Prohibited Data Practices
items: Entering student names, ID numbers, or photographs into public AI platforms
Sharing assessment results or academic records with non-approved AI tools
Using AI to make automated decisions about student placement or intervention without human review
Storing AI conversation logs containing student information on personal devices

content.title: 7.14.4 Professional Development Framework
content.text:
Good AI integration needs steady, planned investment in staff skills. School leaders should run a structured professional development program.

**AI Competency Levels:**

content.title: Foundation Level (All Teaching Staff)
items: Basic understanding of AI capabilities and limitations
Ability to use approved tools for lesson planning and material creation
Knowledge of data privacy requirements and academic integrity policies
Skills in checking and improving AI-generated content
Expected timeline: All staff reach foundation level within the first year of implementation

content.title: Practitioner Level (Teachers Progressing in AI Integration)
items: Advanced prompt writing (prompt engineering) for complex teaching tasks
Using AI tools within differentiated instruction strategies
Using AI to develop assessments and produce feedback
Ability to guide students in responsible AI use
Expected timeline: The majority of staff reach practitioner level within two years

content.title: Leader Level (Department Heads, Senior Teachers, Instructional Coaches)
items: Ability to mentor colleagues in using AI well
Skills in evaluating new AI tools for educational suitability
Ability to lead professional development sessions on AI topics
Contribution to school and network policy development
Expected timeline: Leader level is not an early-stage target. Identified teacher leaders may develop to this level over about 24-36 months. Not all teachers are expected to reach it

content.title: Professional Development Delivery Methods
items: Network-wide training sessions coordinated by the office of the Eduversal Chief Academic Officer
School-based professional learning communities focused on AI integration
Online self-directed learning modules and resources
Peer observation and collaborative planning sessions
External workshops and conferences where appropriate

content.title: Documentation and Recognition
items: Keep records of staff participation in AI professional development
Include AI competency development in teacher appraisal discussions
Recognize and celebrate effective AI integration practices
Create opportunities for skilled teachers to share expertise across the network

content.title: 7.14.5 Quality Assurance and Monitoring
content.text:
School leaders must set up ways to monitor the quality of AI integration and to make sure it matches educational objectives.

**Classroom Observation Focus Areas:**

When observers watch lessons that use AI, they should consider:

content.title: Pedagogical Purpose
items: Is AI being used to support specific learning objectives?
Does the AI use match the lesson's educational goals?
Does using AI add clear value?

content.title: Quality of Implementation
items: Has AI-generated content been properly checked and improved?
Is the teacher using professional judgment when using AI?
Are students actively engaged in learning, not just passively taking in AI output?

content.title: Student Learning Impact
items: Are students developing understanding and skills, not just receiving AI-generated answers?
Is AI supporting differentiation for the different needs of learners?
Are students taught to judge AI-assisted work critically?

content.text:
Observation feedback should discuss AI integration in a helpful way, by recognizing effective practice and naming areas for growth.

**School-Level Monitoring:**

content.title: Regular Review Meetings
items: Discussion of AI integration progress at leadership meetings every term
Department-level sharing of effective practices and challenges
Collecting and analyzing feedback from students and parents

content.title: Data Collection
items: Track participation in professional development and progress through competency levels
Monitor academic integrity incidents related to AI
Collect teachers' self-assessments of how confident they are with AI and how often they use it

content.title: Annual Review
items: A full review of AI integration progress against the strategic plan
Analysis of impact on teacher workload and student outcomes
Recommendations for changes to policy and practice

content.title: Network-Level Quality Assurance
items: Eduversal School Appraisal may sample AI-related evidence within the existing five domains (D1-D5) where it is relevant. AI integration is not a separate appraisal focus, domain or score
Cross-school sharing of effective practices through principal meetings and network forums
Annual network report on AI integration progress and recommendations

content.title: 7.14.6 Equity and Inclusion in AI Integration
content.text:
AI integration must support fair access to quality education for all students. School leaders are responsible for making sure the benefits of AI reach all learners.

**Access Equity:**

content.title: Infrastructure Equity
items: Make sure reliable internet and suitable devices are available for all classes
Give priority in resource allocation to closing gaps in access
Give students who lack technology at home access at school

content.title: Teacher Capacity Equity
items: Support all teachers in developing AI competencies, not only early adopters
Give extra support to teachers who find it hard to use technology in their teaching
Make sure all staff can access professional development

content.title: Student Opportunity Equity
items: Check whether AI-supported teaching reaches all student groups equally
Deal with any new gaps in AI-related learning opportunities
Make sure extracurricular AI activities are accessible to diverse students

content.title: English as Extra Language Students
items: Use AI tools for vocabulary development, translation support and language scaffolding
Use AI to create differentiated reading materials at appropriate language levels
Make sure the use of AI does not disadvantage students who are still developing their English

content.title: Students with Special Educational Needs
items: Include suitable AI tools in Individual Education Plans
Use AI for creating personalized learning materials and accommodations
Make sure accessibility features are used in AI-supported teaching

content.title: High-Ability Students
items: Use AI to provide extension activities and advanced challenges
Teach advanced AI literacy skills to students who are ready for deeper work
Avoid using AI in ways that reduce intellectual challenge for capable learners

content.title: Addressing Algorithmic Bias
items: Train staff to recognize potential bias in AI-generated content
Review AI outputs for cultural appropriateness and representation
Adapt AI-generated materials to reflect Indonesian contexts and diverse perspectives
Report concerns about biased AI outputs to tool providers and the Eduversal network

content.title: 7.14.7 Communication and Community Engagement
content.text:
Effective AI integration requires clear communication with all stakeholders.

**Parent and Guardian Communication:**

content.title: Initial Communication
items: Inform parents about the school's approach to AI integration
Explain the educational benefits and safeguards in place
Deal with common concerns in advance (academic integrity, screen time, data privacy)
Give opportunities for questions and feedback

content.title: Ongoing Updates
items: Include AI-related updates in regular school communications
Share examples of effective AI-enhanced learning
Tell parents about any important changes to AI policies or tools

content.title: Parent Education
items: Consider offering information sessions on AI in education
Provide resources for parents on supporting responsible AI use at home
Take into account that different generations differ in how familiar and comfortable they are with AI

content.title: Clear Expectations
items: Make sure all students understand AI use policies (see Section 7.13)
Explain expectations at the start of the year and repeat them regularly
Make policies accessible and age-appropriate

content.title: Student Voice
items: Gather student feedback on AI integration experiences
Include student perspectives in policy review processes
Help students act as partners in responsible AI use

content.title: Policy Clarity
items: Make sure all staff can access and understand AI policies
Provide regular updates on approved tools and practice guidance
Create channels for staff questions and concerns

content.title: Collaborative Development
items: Involve teachers in AI policy development and review
Value teachers' practical expertise when shaping how AI is introduced
Build a culture of shared learning and experimentation

content.title: 7.14.8 Policy Review and Continuous Improvement
content.text: AI technology and best practice change quickly. School leaders must make sure policies and practices stay current and effective.

content.title: Review Schedule
items: A full policy review every year (aligned with the school-year planning cycle)
Check-ins every term on implementation progress and new issues
Extra reviews when important new developments happen (new tools, regulatory changes, incidents)

content.title: Review Process
items: Gather input from teachers, students, parents, and leadership
Analyze monitoring data and incident reports
Review developments in AI technology and educational research
Compare against Cambridge International guidance and similar schools
Propose and approve policy updates through appropriate governance channels

content.title: Documentation
items: Maintain version history of AI policies
Record the reasons for important policy changes
Make sure updated policies are shared quickly and are easy to access

content.title: Continuous Improvement Culture
items: Encourage experimentation within policy boundaries
Learn from both successes and setbacks
Share learning across the Eduversal network
Stay connected to broader developments in AI and education

subsections.title: Managing Student Behavior and Positive Discipline

content.text: Create safe, respectful and productive learning environments. Do this through proactive behavior management, culturally responsive discipline and restorative practices. These practices build student accountability and relationships.
content.title: Purpose

content.text: Set Clear Expectations from Day One
content.title: 7.15.1 Proactive Behavior Management

items.text: Develop classroom norms together with students (when students feel ownership, they accept the norms more)
items: Example norms: "Respect each other's ideas," "One person speaks at a time," "Arrive on time with materials," "Mistakes are opportunities to learn"
Display the norms where everyone can see them, and refer to them regularly
Teach behavior expectations clearly and directly; do not just state them
Show what "active listening" looks like, and practice transitions
Greet students at the door, use their names and make eye contact
Show interest in students' lives beyond academics
2x10 Strategy: Spend 2 minutes a day, for 10 days in a row, talking with a challenging student about their interests. This builds the relationship and reduces behavior issues
Recognize that behavior often shows an unmet need (tired, hungry, anxious, confused, or looking for attention or belonging)
Bored, confused, or unchallenged students misbehave more
Vary activities (no more than 10-15 minutes on one activity for younger students)
Active learning strategies keep students engaged
Clear learning goals help students understand the purpose of their work
Consistent routines for entering class, moving between activities, handing out materials, handing in work and leaving class
Routines reduce disorder and help students feel safe, especially EAL students and students with SEN
Practice routines until automatic
Notice and praise students who are doing the right thing: "I notice the whole group is collaborating respectfully—great job!"
Specific praise: "Maria, your thoughtful question pushed our discussion deeper" (not just a general "good job")
Praise in public, correct in private (do not embarrass students in front of their classmates)

content.text: Misbehavior will happen; it is a normal part of adolescence. When it happens, respond calmly, consistently and respectfully. Least Invasive to Most Invasive Responses (Graduated Approach): Level 1: Non-Verbal Interventions (for minor off-task behavior)
content.title: 7.15.2 Responding to Misbehavior

items: Proximity: Move near the student and stand close by while you teach
Eye contact: A short look that says "I see you; refocus"
Gesture: Point to the work or tap the desk gently as a reminder
Pause: Stop speaking and wait for attention before you continue

content.text: Level 2: Verbal Reminders (for continued off-task behavior)

items: Private, quiet redirection: Lean down and speak softly: "Let's focus on task, please"
Remind students of the norms: "Remember our norm: One speaker at a time"
Offer a choice: "You can continue working here quietly, or move to different seat to refocus. Your choice."

content.text: Level 3: Logical Consequences (for disruptive or repeated behavior)

items: Loss of a privilege linked to the behavior: if a student misuses materials, they lose access to them for a short time
Time-out or break: The student leaves the situation for a short time to calm down (this is not a punishment; it helps the student reset)
Repair harm: if a student damages property, they help fix or clean it; if a student hurts someone's feelings, they apologize

content.text: Level 4: Referral to Leadership (for serious or persistent behavior)

items: Serious offenses: Physical aggression, defiance, bullying, unsafe behavior
Persistent issues: after several recorded interventions have not improved the behavior
School counselor/student support: for behavior that comes from emotional, social or trauma-related issues

content.text: Restorative Conversations (For Relationship Harm): When a student's behavior hurts others, use restorative questions (not a lecture that punishes):

steps: What happened? (Student's perspective)
Who was affected by your actions? How?
What needs to happen to make things right?
What will you do differently next time?

content.text: Purpose: To build accountability and empathy, and to repair relationships (not just to punish).
Recognize Cultural Differences in Communication and Behavior:
content.title: 7.15.3 Culturally Responsive Discipline

items: Eye Contact: In some Indonesian and Muslim cultures, avoiding eye contact with authority figures shows respect. It is not defiance or dishonesty, as people in Western contexts might think
Group vs. Individual Orientation: Indonesian students may be more collectivist (group-focused). Public shaming is especially damaging. Group accountability strategies can be effective
Respect for Authority: Students may not question teachers openly, even when they are confused. Silence does not mean agreement or understanding
Research shows that students from marginalized groups are disciplined more often than other students for subjective behaviors (defiance, disrespect, disruption)

items.text: Check Your Assumptions: Is this behavior actually disruptive, or just different from my cultural norms?
items: Example: A student who speaks loudly and uses expressive gestures during group work may be showing a home communication style, not disrespect
Apply discipline in the same way to all students. Watch your own patterns (Who am I sending out of class most often? Why?)
Some students have experienced trauma (poverty, violence, loss, displacement)
Trauma can show up as behavior problems (fight/flight/freeze responses, difficulty controlling emotions, hypervigilance or always being on alert)
Respond with compassion and structure: "I see you're struggling today. Let's take a break. When you're ready, we'll work together to solve this."

content.text: The following practices are STRICTLY PROHIBITED in all Eduversal Partner Schools:
content.title: 7.15.4 Prohibited Discipline Practices

items: Physical punishment of any kind (hitting, slapping, pulling, pushing)
Humiliation or shaming (mocking, sarcasm, name-calling, public ridicule)
Excessive tasks or tasks given as punishment (writing "I will not..." 100 times, excessive homework as punishment)
Withholding meals, bathroom access, or recess (basic needs cannot be used as punishment)
Isolation for long periods without supervision
Any punishment that violates student dignity or rights

content.text:
If You Witness Prohibited Practices: Report them immediately to the Principal or Academic Coordinator (See Safeguarding Policy, Section 9).

Alternatives to Punitive Discipline: Use logical consequences, restorative practices, behavior contracts and work with the counselor or parents. Teach students replacement behaviors.

See the Student Handbook for the full Behavior Management Policy and disciplinary procedures.
Recognize that teacher wellbeing directly affects teaching quality and student outcomes. Sustainable teaching practices prevent burnout and support long-term career satisfaction.
content.title: Purpose

items: Not everything can be perfect. Identify the tasks that have the most impact

items.text: Use the 80/20 rule: Focus on the 20% of effort that brings 80% of the results
items: Example: Detailed feedback on a major essay has high impact. Grading every homework assignment with long comments has lower impact—spot-check instead
Grade all essays in 2-3 set sessions, not at random times
Respond to all parent emails in one time block
Plan lessons for the entire week in one planning session
Lesson plan template saves time
Email templates for common communications (parent updates, absence follow-ups)
Classroom routines reduce the need to make decisions all the time
Plan together with colleagues (share the work)
Share resources in PLCs; use what colleagues have already made
Ask for help when overwhelmed
Set your work hours and tell parents about them (respond to non-urgent emails within 24-48 hours during the school week, not immediately)
Keep weekends for rest and family (at least one full day without school work)
Learn to say "no" to extra commitments when you already have as much work as you can manage
Use Google Classroom or an LMS (Learning Management System) to make assignment submission and organization simpler
Auto-grade objective questions (multiple choice, fill-in-blank) where appropriate
Voice-to-text for comments (faster than typing)
Sleep: Aim for 7-8 hours (a long-term lack of sleep harms judgment and patience)
Nutrition: Do not skip meals; keep healthy snacks in the classroom
Exercise: Even 20-30 minutes a day reduces stress and improves mood
Hydration: Drink water throughout day (keep water bottle at desk)
Practice stress management: Deep breathing, mindfulness, meditation (apps like Headspace, Calm)
Stay in contact with supportive colleagues; do not cut yourself off when you are struggling
Get professional support if needed (counseling, therapy). This is not a sign of weakness
Celebrate small wins. Teaching is hard, and progress is not always visible right away
Maintain hobbies and interests outside teaching
Spend time with family and friends
Travel, read for pleasure, create, play—whatever brings you joy
Remember your identity beyond "teacher"

items.text: Eduversal Partner Schools are encouraged to provide:
items: Reasonable teaching loads (contact hours, class sizes)
Adequate planning time
Professional development on wellbeing
Access to counseling or EAP (Employee Assistance Program)
Collegial, supportive culture
Persistent feelings of anxiety, depression, hopelessness
Difficulty sleeping or concentrating
Physical symptoms of stress (headaches, stomach issues, frequent illness)
Thoughts of leaving the profession even though you love teaching
Feeling unable to cope with daily demands

content.text: Resources: Speak with Principal, counselor, or HR about support options. Mental health is as important as physical health.

content.title: Appendix 7-A: Teacher Appraisal Rubrics (Detailed Indicators)
content.text: The rubric set has approximately 24 indicators across the four appraisal domains. Each indicator is written at four performance levels. The full set is not reproduced here. The sample below shows the format; every other indicator follows the same three-column structure. Teachers are expected to demonstrate Proficient (Level 3) performance across all indicators. This is the baseline for effective teaching.
Domain 2 - Classroom Observation, Sub-Domain 2c: Instructional Process. Indicator: Uses Questioning and Discussion Techniques.

content.title: Appendix 7-A Sample Rubric — Domain 2c: Uses Questioning and Discussion Techniques
rows: Teacher's questions are mostly low-level (recall); few students take part in discussions; teacher does not probe or scaffold responses
Questions limited to "what" and "who"; teacher accepts first answer without probing; same students answer repeatedly; minimal wait time
Teacher asks a mix of low and higher-level questions, but most are still low-level; some attempt to engage multiple students
Some analysis or application questions asked; teacher occasionally probes responses ("Can you explain why?"); inconsistent wait time; 40-60% of students participate
Teacher asks varied questions (recall, analysis, evaluation); uses wait time well; engages most students in discussion; probes and scaffolds to deepen thinking
Balanced use of Bloom's levels; consistent 5+ second wait time; encourages student-to-student discussion; 70-85% participation; follows up on student responses to extend thinking
Teacher facilitates student-led discussions; students ask each other higher-order questions; discourse is thoughtful, respectful, and intellectually rigorous; all students engaged

Students initiate questions and challenge each other's ideas respectfully; teacher acts as facilitator, not primary questioner; genuine inquiry and debate; 90%+ participation; norms for academic discourse evident
